Recoverable Symbols, Unstable Execution:
Auditing Internal Pathways and Decision Identity
in Visual State Tracking

Ruiqi Liu1,2   Jinming Li2   Mo Wang3,4,∗   Yang Lu2,∗   Yanlan Kang1,∗

1Institute of Medical Philosophy & Future AI (IMPF-AI)

2Fudan University  3The University of Warwick  4Southern University of Science and Technology

∗Corresponding authors

Abstract

Visual features can retain every symbol a task needs while a model built on them still changes its answer when irrelevant parts of the image change. We study this gap in visual state tracking, where a recurrent executor reads a sequence of symbol tiles through a frozen ViT encoder and decides whether a displayed candidate equals the final state. Our diagnostic pairs each input with a donor view that preserves every queried tile, checks with a symbol-supervised decoder that the full symbol chain is recoverable from both feature sequences, and swaps individual internal channels of the same fitted executor in both directions. On 3,526 pairs in which every symbol is recovered in both views, changing the surrounding context lowers the balanced accuracy of a rotary recurrent head by 17.13 points. The loss runs mainly through the input-dependent rotation phase: restoring the original phase repairs 351 of 391 new errors and brings accuracy back to 88.54%, yet 142 individual predictions still differ from the original ones. A locked test on 192 unseen program families reproduces the pathway (28 of 29 new errors repaired; 382 of 384 predictions unchanged), and the effect partly carries over to single-image canvases. Consistency objectives derived from this analysis reduce the internal discrepancy they target but do not outperform ordinary data augmentation.

1 Introduction

Visual state tracking requires a model to read a sequence of symbols, apply their operations and compare the resulting state with a candidate. A wrong answer can arise at any of these stages. Recognition and execution are therefore different objects of evaluation, even when they share the same visual representation. A representation may retain every required symbol while the computation built on it remains sensitive to surrounding content. Fig. 1 shows an example.

Aggregate scores can conceal which decisions changed. An internal intervention may restore accuracy by correcting some examples while making others wrong. Paired inputs provide the reference needed to distinguish restored correctness from recovered original predictions.

Consider a program whose queried symbols and their positions stay fixed while other visible tiles change. A global encoder can change its features at the preserved queries because those features integrate the surrounding image. The question is what the learned executor does with this change. If every symbol can still be recovered from both feature sequences, a missing symbol cannot explain a changed answer, and the cause has to be sought in the executor.

Existing work already separates recognition from tracking, compares local and contextual inputs, and studies recurrent error dynamics [15, 5, 4]. These studies measure recognition and execution on different inputs or interfaces. We measure both on the same paired instances and inside the same fitted executor.

We introduce a paired diagnostic for this purpose. It combines query-preserving interventions, complete-chain recovery and bidirectional substitutions of the executor’s channels. A symbol-supervised decoder supplies an information witness, while the task head continues to operate on its original feature inputs. Injection asks whether a donor channel reproduces the execution loss. Restoration asks whether replacing that channel with its original value reverses the loss. Testing both directions separates a channel the computation depends on from one that merely changes along with it.

We report two main findings. First, complete symbol recovery coexists with a large execution loss, and a phase pathway accounts for most new errors in capable G5c Rotary heads. Second, restoring average balanced accuracy leaves individual predictions changed, so we report the errors an intervention repairs, the errors it introduces and its agreement with the original decisions. A locked test on new program families confirms the phase pathway.

The contributions are:

  • •

    A query-preserving diagnostic that verifies complete symbol recovery and tests the same fitted executor on paired features.

  • •

    Bidirectional channel interventions, confirmed on new program families, that locate a phase-sensitive pathway in capable Rotary heads.

  • •

    Decision-level recovery accounting and shared-canvas and training comparisons that test the pathway’s explanatory and practical scope.

2 Related Work

Local perception and sequential tracking.

Madan et al. [15] study locality, shortcuts and length generalization with heads receiving common local streams. MET-Bench [5] separates action recognition from entity tracking through a text interface. These works motivate testing the information presented to a sequential computation. We add a complete recovery witness on each paired instance and intervene within the same fitted executor. Background composites isolate recognition-context effects [21]; the surrounding program tiles here retain semantics and are called non-query content. Globally contextual ViT features [7] make preserved-pixel interventions informative about downstream execution.

Recoverability and internal interventions.

Probing distinguishes information accessible to a decoder from information used by a decision rule [2, 9]. Visual counterfactuals examine binding and recognized geometry [6, 8]. Activation substitutions and interchange training provide tools for testing computational pathways [10, 23, 11]. We combine these approaches with paired complete-program recovery and explicit error transitions. CVRR makes recurrent state a required image-conditioned route to the answer [18]; our analysis follows the transition, write and readout routes already present in a fitted head.

Recurrent dynamics and consistency learning.

DeltaProduct motivates the one- and two-factor controls [12, 19]. Rotary uses a block-rotation parameterization related to Mamba-3 within a simpler architecture [14]. Chung et al. [4] analyze state-separating error, readability and finite failure horizons. We trace the additional changes induced by visual context through a fitted computation. The affine expansion organizes measurements of injection and propagation; the readout connects them to decisions. Augmentation and counterfactual invariance [13, 20] provide training comparisons for constraints derived from this diagnosis.

3 Method: Paired Diagnostics for Visual State Tracking

Programs and task semantics.

A program specifies a start state s0s_{0}, operations a1:Ta_{1:T} and candidate ee. For grammar transition πg,a\pi_{g,a},

st=πg,at(st−1),y=𝟏{sT=e}.s_{t}=\pi_{g,a_{t}}(s_{t-1}),\qquad y=\mathbf{1}\{s_{T}=e\}. (1)

G5c applies increments {1,−1,2,−2,0}\{1,-1,2,-2,0\} in ℤ5\mathbb{Z}_{5}. For example, start 1 followed by +2,−1,0+2,-1,0 ends at 2, making candidate 2 legal and candidate 3 illegal. Identity operations are rendered and processed like other inputs. G5r uses overlapping cycles (j​j+1​j+2)(j\ j+1\ j+2) for j=0,1,2j=0,1,2, making operation order consequential. The grammars also differ in vocabulary and transition frequency.

The rendered 448×112448\times 112 canvas contains 32-pixel tiles. A frozen DINOv2-S/14 [17] or DINOv1-S/16 [3] encoder supplies 384-dimensional features at known query centers. The supplied traversal orders the start, operations and candidate. Training contains 3–7 nonidentity operations; primary longer tests contain 8–10. Abstract-program partitioning removes identities and includes negative examples’ source programs. Each full-budget block uses 16,000 training and 6,000 validation images, 5,040 updates, legality supervision and auxiliary state supervision. Blocks jointly vary data and initialization.

The operation sequence determines the final state, and the displayed candidate determines which comparison is asked, so the same program appears with both labels. Known query centers and traversal remove visual search, leaving representation and sequential updates. The candidate is still a visual input: its contextual feature affects the memory update, the query used to read memory and the classifier residual, so we also intervene on it separately.

The fitted executor.

The matrix heads first standardize features using training-only statistics. A learned projection to width 128, a width-one depthwise convolution and SiLU produce utu_{t}. The main Rotary head has four 22×2222\times 22 memories. Each head projects a unit query qtq_{t}, unit key ktk_{t}, value vtv_{t}, decay ρt=σ⁡(Wρ​ut+bρ)\rho_{t}=\sigma(W_{\rho}u_{t}+b_{\rho}) and eleven angles θt=π​tanh⁡(Wθ​ut+bθ)\theta_{t}=\pi\tanh(W_{\theta}u_{t}+b_{\theta}). Its update is

St=St−1​At+Bt,At=ρt​R​(θt),Bt=vt​kt⊤,S_{t}=S_{t-1}A_{t}+B_{t},\quad A_{t}=\rho_{t}R(\theta_{t}),\quad B_{t}=v_{t}k_{t}^{\top}, (2)

with zero initial memory and block-diagonal planar rotations. Queries qtq_{t} are continuous readout vectors; sts_{t} in Eq. 1 denotes the discrete task state.

Concatenating St​qtS_{t}q_{t} across heads gives rtr_{t}. The model forms ot=Wo​LN⁡(rt)+bo+uto_{t}=W_{o}\operatorname{LN}(r_{t})+b_{o}+u_{t} and classifies [on;un][o_{n};u_{n}] with a two-layer GELU MLP at the candidate node nn. A linear auxiliary readout predicts states from oto_{t}. Thus the candidate updates memory before classification, and the residual enters both ono_{n} and the classifier input. The 2F control uses four 16×1616\times 16 memories and two successive delta updates S←S−β⁡(S​k−v)​k⊤S\leftarrow S-\beta(Sk-v)k^{\top}, with unit keys and β∈(0,2)\beta\in(0,2). GRU supplies a nonlinear recurrent control. Appendix A.2 gives complete equations, dimensions and selection protocols.

For a valid sequence, the optimized loss combines binary legality cross-entropy with auxiliary state cross-entropy of weight 1/21/2. Auxiliary supervision covers the start and operation nodes, with identities inheriting the preceding state; the displayed candidate and padding are excluded. The primary recurrence processes every valid node in order, including identities. At evaluation, both views use the same fitted parameters and training-derived feature scaling. The interventions therefore change only the inputs or chosen internal channels of a fixed computation.

Query-preserving construction.

For each node tt, we copy its tile and absolute position into a matched donor canvas, encode that canvas and sample only its query feature ztDz_{t}^{D} (Fig. 1). The assembled donor sequence ZD=(ztD)tZ^{D}=(z_{t}^{D})_{t} therefore combines separately encoded canvases. Its label remains that of the preserved source-symbol chain. Donors match split, node count, carrier and vocabulary. We compare the same fitted head on the original F and donor D sequences, fixing normalization, readout and decision threshold.

Initial sampling support is audited separately. DINOv2 bilinear sampling extends 2–4 pixels beyond the tile at eight of thirteen positions, including two that reach blank space. DINOv1 sampling lies inside the preserved tile, so its initial sampled embeddings are identical across views. This second encoder tests whether sensitivity persists with unchanged initial support.

Later attention layers can still propagate distant differences. The shared-canvas protocol in Sec. 4.4 instead obtains every target query from one image and one encoder pass.

Complete recovery witness.

Role-specific ridge decoders learn start, operation and candidate identities from full-context training tokens; original validation tokens select regularization. An exact grammar executor then evaluates their decoded chain. A pair is jointly exact when every symbol is correct in both views. This demands complete recovery, including intermediate operations and the candidate, so compensating token errors cannot explain the selected pair’s exactness.

The witness and task head are parallel readouts of the same features. The witness receives symbol supervision and known transition rules. The learned executor receives legality and auxiliary states and must learn its own use of the representation. Complete recovery thus shows that the information needed for exact execution is present in both feature sequences; the executor’s decisions on these pairs show whether it uses that information consistently.

Interventions and estimands.

We exchange a named channel while keeping all other channels at their recipient values. Donor injection uses F as recipient; original restoration uses D. Both operation and candidate nodes enter full phase exchange. We report balanced accuracy (BA), the mean of classwise recalls, along with corrected errors, introduced errors and disagreement with F. Eight-block estimates weight blocks equally; paired intervals resample whole blocks unless specified otherwise. Jointly exact subsets condition on the decoding outcomes.

Corrected and introduced errors compare the intervention with its recipient using the true label. Disagreement with F tracks prediction identity independently of correctness. Repairs of newly induced donor errors test reversal of the original failure. On class-balanced panels, accuracy equals within-block BA; sensitivity exclusions require classwise recomputation.

4 Experiments

4.1 Confirmation on new program families

We start with the locked confirmation (Fig. 2). Eight existing DINOv1 Rotary checkpoints and their decoders were frozen before encoding 192 new canonical families. Each family supplies legal and illegal candidates, giving 384 instances over eight blocks. All families are disjoint from retained training, validation and previous test families. Original BA ranges from 95.83% to 100%, and all 384 pairs have complete recovery in both views.

New-family generation is performed after the model and decoder files, exclusion rules and intervention protocol are fixed. Canonicalization removes identity operations, normalizes operation names by first occurrence, and identifies forward/reversed normalized sequences. The family exclusion union includes retained historical training, validation and test programs as well as source programs used to construct negative candidates. Uncertainty is evaluated across the eight fixed training/program blocks.

Original BA is 99.22% and donor BA is 92.19% (−7.03-7.03 pp, 95% CI [−11.46,−2.60][-11.46,-2.60]). Injecting donor phase yields 92.97%. Restoring original phase within D yields 98.70%, repairs 28/29 new donor errors and introduces three errors relative to D. Two of 384 predictions still differ from F. The pathway thus carries over to unseen programs, and here too repair is not the same as exact recovery of predictions. Removing the thirteen within-family donor assignments leaves 371 pairs, a −7.30-7.30 pp donor effect and the same 28/29 repairs, three introduced errors and two disagreements (Appendix G.1).

4.2 Complete recovery retains an execution gap

The larger recovery panel contains 3,840 paired inputs, 480 per block. Donor replacement changes G5c Rotary BA from 88.80% to 71.80% (−17.01-17.01 pp, [−19.21,−13.73][-19.21,-13.73]). Among 3,526 jointly exact pairs, original and donor BA are 89.18% and 72.06%: the effect remains −17.13-17.13 pp ([−19.26,−13.60][-19.26,-13.60]). The loss is unchanged when every symbol is recovered in both views. Intervals resample blocks and donor-linked components to preserve the paired dependence.

A composition-control panel uses 960 source programs, 120 per block. Permuting the same operation multiset changes BA by only −0.08-0.08 pp on the composition-control panel. Changing surrounding operation values while preserving their modular sum, identity mask and state tiles changes BA by −10.14-10.14 pp ([−12.26,−8.26][-12.26,-8.26]), or −9.64-9.64 pp among jointly exact pairs. Preserving the sum holds the surrounding operations’ net modular effect fixed, whereas preserving the multiset also holds their composition fixed. Their contrast identifies composition sensitivity beyond the net effect.

Same-symbol rerendering changes only appearance, and state-tile changes affect only the start and endpoint tiles; both have smaller effects (Fig. 3). The executor is therefore sensitive to the composition of the surrounding operations. Direction tests for more specific shortcuts are in Appendix A.6.

The 1,920-pair channel panel supplies the same paired inputs to the learned controls. Table 1 shows that 2F and GRU incur smaller accuracy losses and fewer prediction changes than Rotary. They still change 7.19% and 3.85% of decisions. Full capability, parameter and budget comparisons are in Appendix A.3. The composition and channel panels reuse sources from the recovery panel and overlap on 497 rows; they test distinct interventions on those sources.

4.3 Bidirectional interventions identify a phase pathway

An exact affine expansion guides the channel measurements. For original F and donor D, define

Et=St−1F​(AtD−AtF)+(BtD−BtF).E_{t}=S_{t-1}^{F}(A_{t}^{D}-A_{t}^{F})+(B_{t}^{D}-B_{t}^{F}). (3)

The state difference satisfies

δn=∑t=1nEt​∏j=t+1nAjD,δt=StD−StF.\delta_{n}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}E_{t}\prod_{j=t+1}^{n}A_{j}^{D},\quad\delta_{t}=S_{t}^{D}-S_{t}^{F}. (4)

It separates newly injected differences from their propagation. For two planar rotation matrices, ‖R⁡(θD)−R⁡(θF)‖2=2​|sin⁡((θD−θF)/2)|\|R(\theta_{D})-R(\theta_{F})\|_{2}=2|\sin((\theta_{D}-\theta_{F})/2)|. The effect on a decision additionally depends on the stored state, later transitions and readout.

On the DINOv2 channel panel, injecting donor phase lowers BA from 88.54% to 72.19%, close to the full donor value of 72.86%. Individual decay, write, query and residual substitutions have smaller effects. In the reverse direction, restoring original phase raises donor BA to 88.54% and fixes 351/391 newly wrong decisions (Fig. 4). The four-cell comparison fixes non-phase channels to F or D while choosing phase from either view. It links both the induced loss and its reversal to the phase pathway under the respective recipient computations.

Restoration corrects 386 donor errors and introduces 85 errors. Relative to F, 71 originally correct answers become wrong and 71 originally wrong answers become correct. Equal BA therefore conceals 142/1,920 changed predictions (7.40%). Recovering the score is therefore not the same as recovering the original outputs. Appendix B gives the full four-cell results and restoration costs.

Role-specific swaps further locate the response. Operation-only restoration repairs 343/391 new errors, compared with 61/391 for the single candidate node. These compare node sets of different sizes. For one head, the candidate update before reading gives

rn,h=Sn−1,h​(An,h​qn,h)+Bn,h​qn,h.r_{n,h}=S_{n-1,h}(A_{n,h}q_{n,h})+B_{n,h}q_{n,h}. (5)

Candidate phase thus changes the effective query applied to accumulated memory. The normalized readout, residual and classifier convert the resulting change into a final margin. DINOv1 tests on the same channel-panel RGB inputs reach 99.58% original and 92.86% donor BA with complete recovery; full phase restoration repairs all 134 new errors and reproduces the original predictions.

4.4 Shared canvases and partial phase transfer

The query-specific protocol assembles features from multiple canvases. We therefore train new heads in a fixed two-row layout with a target program and a distractor. Each view samples a distractor from the same balanced law, while keeping all target pixels and query positions fixed. All target features in a view come from one encoder pass. D0 and D1 are symmetric samples, making prediction disagreement the natural sensitivity measure.

On 2,432 length-seven pairs, DINOv2 Rotary scores 91.04% and 91.37% BA and changes 214 decisions (8.80%, [6.95,10.69][6.95,10.69]). Among 2,053 jointly exact pairs, 153 still disagree (7.45%, [5.65,9.38][5.65,9.38]). DINOv1 answers every length-seven pair correctly. At length ten, DINOv1 reaches 98.05% and 97.99% BA with 24/3,840 disagreements and complete recovery. Figure 5 shows all twelve encoder/head/length conditions.

The mechanism transfers partially. Among the 153 jointly exact DINOv2 length-seven disagreements, exchanging all phase makes only 60 predictions follow D1 when D0 is the recipient, and 70 follow D0 in the reverse direction. These counts measure how often the prediction follows the source, not corrected errors. In coherent images the gap between recoverability and stability remains, but phase explains only part of it.

4.5 From internal restoration to training objectives

The original four adaptation arms share checkpoints, 2,000 training rows, 480 validation rows and 256 updates. Clean ERM, donor augmentation, output consistency and counterfactual transport consistency (CTC) receive matched task-loss evaluations. CTC penalizes normalized innovation in Eq. 3 using a stop-gradient original trajectory. A later read/residual transport objective (RTC) covers the interface feeding the classifier. Table 2 summarizes the original and later training signals; Appendix F.3 gives formulas, validation selection and costs.

Augmentation gains 5.16 pp donor BA and loses 3.44 pp original BA relative to clean ERM. CTC reduces held-out innovation discrepancy in every block but adds only +0.16+0.16 pp donor BA over augmentation ([−0.73,1.09][-0.73,1.09]). In a full-budget rerun with validation-selected weights and 1,920 new rows from 960 families, augmentation yields 74.95%/67.76% original/donor BA, CTC 74.84%/67.40%, and RTC 74.17%/66.61%. Both objectives reduce the discrepancy they target but do not improve accuracy over augmentation.

A two-block DINOv1 validation pilot tests a more direct constraint: predicting operation phase from local pixels makes the angles exactly invariant across views. Replacing those angles by a pooled constant reduces original BA to 48.1% and 52.1%. Execution therefore depends on input-varying operation phase in these fitted heads. Nevertheless, restoring original writes raises donor BA from 65.21% to 83.54% in one block and from 98.13% to 100% in the other. Making phase invariant thus leaves a write pathway open. The pilot stopped at validation (Appendix H).

5 Discussion

Complete recovery changes what a contextual failure means. If a decoder reads every symbol from both feature sequences, the encoder has not lost the information; the failure lies in how the learned executor uses it. Probing work separates decodability from use [2, 9]; the paired construction measures both on the same instances.

In capable G5c Rotary heads, most of the contextual loss passes through the rotation phase: injecting donor phase reproduces it and restoring the original phase removes it, on the channel panel and on new program families. Phase acts on stored memory together with decay, writes and readout, so its effect depends on the recipient computation. In shared canvases phase explains only part of the disagreements, and the other channels need the same analysis.

Implications for training.

Fixing one channel does not make the executor robust. When operation phase is computed from local pixels, it agrees across views, yet the refitted head still depends on how phase varies with the input and becomes sensitive through its writes instead. Penalizing local state innovation reduces its average size but protects neither a small classification margin nor the query and residual paths. The readout bound in Appendix B.2 makes these terms explicit. Margin-aware weighting and joint constraints on update, state and readout are natural next objectives, with ordinary augmentation as the baseline.

Reporting decisions, not only scores.

A restored score can hide repaired and newly introduced errors that cancel. 2F and GRU lose less accuracy but still change 7.19% and 3.85% of decisions. We therefore report error transitions and paired agreement next to BA. Keeping every original answer is not always desirable, since some original answers were wrong; the counts make this trade-off visible.

Limitations.

All experiments use generated symbols, a supplied traversal and frozen encoders. The query-specific and shared-canvas protocols differ in both training and context distribution, and the two encoders differ in pretraining and patch geometry. The local-phase study covers two validation blocks. Natural scenes, unknown transition rules and capable VLMs are left for future work.

6 Conclusion

A visual executor can fail on inputs from which every needed symbol is recoverable. In capable rotary heads this failure runs mainly through the input-dependent phase, as shown by injection and restoration on both analyzed and unseen programs. Restoring accuracy does not restore the original predictions, so decision-level counts should accompany aggregate scores in this kind of analysis.

GPT through Codex assisted with language polishing and routine code completion. The authors verified the manuscript and code against the recorded methods and results and take responsibility for all content.

Appendix Overview

This appendix gives the protocols, full numerical results and additional controls behind the main text. All trained blocks and comparison arms are reported, including low-capability conditions. Unless stated otherwise, the eight paired training/program blocks are the independent units, intervals are paired 95% whole-block bootstrap intervals, accuracy is balanced accuracy (BA) in percent, and differences are in percentage points (pp). Table A1 maps each result in the main text to its supporting material.

Panels and notation.

We use the panel names of the main text. The recovery panel contains 3,840 archived G5c pairs (480 per block). The composition-control panel contains 960 of its source programs (120 per block). The channel panel contains 240 pairs per block and grammar (1,920 per grammar); it supports the channel substitutions and the complete context matrix, and its G5c rows share 497 source programs with the composition-control panel (Fig. A1). The new-family confirmation contains 384 pairs from 192 unseen canonical families (Sec. G). F denotes the original view and D the query-preserving donor view; V, S, P and P+ are the further context interventions of Sec. A.4. G5c and G5r are the two five-state grammars, and Rotary, 2F, 1F and GRU are the learned heads (Sec. A.2). Decoder + rules denotes the symbol-supervised role decoder followed by exact transitions. It serves as the recovery witness and is labeled “fixed rules”, “probe + rules” or “decoder–executor” in some displays. Flips are the percentage of paired decisions that differ between two views. CTC and RTC are the counterfactual transport-consistency and readout transport-consistency objectives (Secs. C.1 and F.3).

Appendix A Experimental Matrix and Reproducibility

A.1 Data, rendering, and partitions

The original canvas is 448×112448\times 112 pixels. Tile tt is centered at (32+32​t,56)(32+32t,56) and has width 32. Each tile is independently supersampled, jittered, and perturbed with pixel noise. Randomness depends on the rendering seed and node index. A queried tile is copied exactly when its surrounding context changes. The original and isolated renderings use the same operation vocabulary and state carrier. This prevents future semantic states from controlling local rendering noise.

There are 16,000 training, 6,000 validation, 6,000 training-range test, and 6,000 long-chain test images per grammar and block. Training and validation contain 3–7 nonidentity operations; the long-chain split contains 8–10. Abstract operation strings with identities removed are partitioned, including displayed strings and the sources used to generate negative examples. The mean number of distinct displayed training programs is approximately 2,146 for G5r and 6,476 for G5c; long-chain counts are approximately 5,597 and 5,957. Image counts therefore include repeated abstract programs. Blocks are the independent unit in all interval estimates.

DINOv2-S/14 supplies a 384-dimensional feature at each known center. Raw features and earlier standardized caches use half precision. The recurrence uses single precision. Training-node means and standard deviations exclude padding and remain fixed for all validation and intervention inputs. Isolated encoding required approximately 8.8–8.9 times as many canvases and 3.1–3.3 times the encoder time. Cost therefore differs even when the downstream sequence is identical.

A.2 Complete executor definitions

The primary inputs are ordered 384-dimensional frozen-encoder features. Training-only feature means and standard deviations are fixed at evaluation. Matrix heads share a width-128 affine projection, a depthwise convolution with kernel one, and SiLU. Thus ut=SiLU⁡(C⁡(Wz​z~t+bz))u_{t}=\operatorname{SiLU}(C(W_{z}\widetilde{z}_{t}+b_{z})), with a pointwise learned CC. The primary projection has no additional neighboring sequence inputs. Global visual encoding can already transmit contextual information to z~t\widetilde{z}_{t}.

For each matrix head hh, queries and keys are linear projections of utu_{t} normalized to unit Euclidean length; values are unconstrained linear projections. Rotary uses four heads with key and value dimension 22, giving four 22×2222\times 22 zero-initialized memories and an 88-dimensional concatenated read. Each head has eleven input-dependent planar angles and a scalar decay:

θt,h\displaystyle\theta_{t,h} =π​tanh⁡(Wθ,h​ut+bθ,h),\displaystyle=\pi\tanh(W_{\theta,h}u_{t}+b_{\theta,h}), (A1)
ρt,h\displaystyle\rho_{t,h} =σ⁡(Wρ,h​ut+bρ,h),\displaystyle=\sigma(W_{\rho,h}u_{t}+b_{\rho,h}), (A2)
Rh​(θ)\displaystyle R_{h}(\theta) =blockdiagj=111​(cos⁡θjsin⁡θj−sin⁡θjcos⁡θj),\displaystyle=\operatorname{blockdiag}_{j=1}^{11}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_{j}&\sin\theta_{j}\\ -\sin\theta_{j}&\cos\theta_{j}\end{pmatrix}, (A3)
St,h\displaystyle S_{t,h} =ρt,h​St−1,h​Rh​(θt,h)+vt,h​kt,h⊤.\displaystyle=\rho_{t,h}S_{t-1,h}R_{h}(\theta_{t,h})+v_{t,h}k_{t,h}^{\top}. (A4)

The displayed rotation follows the implementation’s row-vector right-multiplication convention. The spectral norm of the difference of two corresponding planar matrices is 2​|sin⁡((θD−θF)/2)|2|\sin((\theta_{D}-\theta_{F})/2)|. Angles and matrix differences are distinct quantities.

The 2F head uses four 16×1616\times 16 memories and two factors at each input. With independently projected kt,h,j,vt,h,jk_{t,h,j},v_{t,h,j} and βt,h,j=2​σ​(Wβ,h,j​ut+bβ,h,j)\beta_{t,h,j}=2\sigma(W_{\beta,h,j}u_{t}+b_{\beta,h,j}), define Aj=I−βj​kj​kj⊤A_{j}=I-\beta_{j}k_{j}k_{j}^{\top} and Bj=βj​vj​kj⊤B_{j}=\beta_{j}v_{j}k_{j}^{\top}. The sequential update is St=(St−1​A1+B1)​A2+B2S_{t}=(S_{t-1}A_{1}+B_{1})A_{2}+B_{2}. Equivalently, its effective affine transition and write are A1​A2A_{1}A_{2} and B1​A2+B2B_{1}A_{2}+B_{2}. The one-factor negative-eigenvalue control has four heads of dimension 24. All valid nodes, including identities, update the memory; padding leaves it unchanged.

The shared matrix-head readout is

rt\displaystyle r_{t} =concath⁡(St,h​qt,h),\displaystyle=\operatorname{concat}_{h}(S_{t,h}q_{t,h}), (A5)
ot\displaystyle o_{t} =Wo​LN⁡(rt)+bo+ut,\displaystyle=W_{o}\operatorname{LN}(r_{t})+b_{o}+u_{t}, (A6)
ℓ\displaystyle\ell =W2​GELU⁡(W1​[on;un]+b1)+b2.\displaystyle=W_{2}\operatorname{GELU}(W_{1}[o_{n};u_{n}]+b_{1})+b_{2}. (A7)

Here WoW_{o} maps the concatenated read to 128 dimensions, W1W_{1} maps 256 to 64 dimensions, and W2W_{2} maps 64 to two legality logits. A linear 40-way auxiliary head reads oto_{t} using the dataset’s shared state-label encoding; the G5 tasks occupy five task states. Start and operation positions contribute auxiliary supervision; the displayed candidate and padding are excluded. The candidate is processed before legality classification. The same unu_{n} contributes through the residual and the separate classifier input.

The primary GRU projects 384 inputs to width 128, applies one unidirectional GRU layer of width 128, and uses linear legality and auxiliary readouts of the last valid and per-node hidden vectors. The parameter-matched GRU uses width 112 for these visual inputs. The full-budget parameter-matched Transformer uses a 384-to-64 input projection, learned positions, two causal pre-normalized layers, four attention heads, width-256 feedforward sublayers, dropout 0.1, and linear task/state readouts. Padding is masked and legality is read at the candidate position. The complete Mamba-1 head and its numerical checks are specified in the training matrix section below. Its reference scan and the simpler rotary head are separate architectures.

A.3 Original and new training matrices

Original blocks pair data seeds 101–108 with initialization seeds 0–7. The full budget is 80 epochs, 5,040 updates, batch 256, AdamW learning rate 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}, weight decay 10−210^{-2} on eligible matrices, gradient clipping at one, and cosine decay following 100 warm-up updates. Legality cross-entropy is augmented by state cross-entropy of weight 1/21/2. Padding and the displayed candidate endpoint are excluded from state supervision. Identity positions inherit the preceding state.

Original model selection uses the latest epoch within max⁡(0.005,p⁡(1−p)/nval)\max(0.005,\sqrt{p(1-p)/n_{\rm val}}) of the best validation BA. The original matrix comprises two grammars, five heads, two contexts, and eight blocks: 160 fits. Its saved predictions were independently recomputed. Table A2 gives the complete matrix, retaining the widened one-factor control.

The short-budget and width controls comprise 896 fits: 384 short-budget architecture cells, 160 additional context-dose cells, 320 additional-backbone cells, and 32 full-budget GRU width controls. Short-budget cells use 2,000 training and 480 validation examples and 512 updates. These runs use different budgets from the full-budget Transformer/Mamba controls.

The full-budget comparisons include 32 Transformer fits, 16 full-budget Mamba-1 fits, 128 frozen-encoder head adaptations, 16 matched encoder-adaptation runs, and eight learning-rate runs. These 200 fits reuse the existing block structure. Jobs ran on two RTX A5000 GPUs; raw probabilities, configurations, validation histories and checkpoints are saved. Frozen replay also records the encoder and checkpoint hashes.

The Mamba head contains two residual pre-LayerNorm blocks of width 80 and state size 16, followed by normalization and task/state readouts. The official Mamba-1 class and official differentiable reference scan are used with source provenance and license preserved. Causal convolution, input-dependent Δ\Delta, BB, and CC, skip DD, and input gate are all present. A numerical gate compares the sequence forward with repeated official step calls; gradients through the input must be finite and nonzero. Runtime describes the differentiable reference implementation; the optimized fused CUDA kernel has a different cost profile.

A.4 Complete context matrix on the channel panel

The channel panel takes the first 40 examples per length/label stratum from each archived deterministic 480-row panel, retaining all eight blocks. The G5c rows contain 8–10 nonidentity operations, 0–3 identities and 10–13 total nodes. The separately generated panels with exactly ten nonidentity operations and one identity use a fixed 13-node composition. Six contexts, four learned heads, and the fixed rule interface are measured on every row. Table A5 reports all five systems, including 1F. The four interfaces in the corrected frozen-comparison family are 2F, Rotary, GRU, and the symbol-supervised fixed decoder–executor. 1F is shown for reference and is not part of that family. Fig. A1 shows how the source panels overlap.

In V, every surrounding nonidentity operation is changed to a different operation using the original rendering seed; the queried tile is restored. The identity mask and operation-region length remain fixed. In S, start and endpoint states are shifted by fixed nonzero offsets before restoring the queried tile. In P, only surrounding nonidentity tiles move. In P+, all surrounding operation-region tiles may move, including identities; nonidentity order can also change. P and P+ preserve the full pixel multiset but can alter spatial statistics. D uses a cyclic donor assignment within split, node count, carrier, and vocabulary. Singleton strata yield seven self-donor programs in G5c and five in G5r. Dropping them changes the G5c Rotary mean donor effect by less than 0.1 pp. This donor seed differs from that of the earlier four-block estimate. Latent feature statistics can covary across these interventions.

A.5 Statistics and multiplicity

BA equals the average of sensitivity and specificity. Each new frozen panel is exactly balanced within every block, so overall accuracy equals BA. We recompute scores using the classwise definition. On the channel panel, paired changes use 20,000 whole-block bootstrap resamples. Exact two-sided sign-flip tests enumerate 2B2^{B} assignments and assume independent blocks with sign-symmetric contrasts under the null. The frozen family comprises 40 contrasts: five perturbations against F, the four interfaces 2F/Rotary/GRU/fixed decoder–executor, and two grammars. 1F and the later Transformer, Mamba-1 and width-matched GRU comparisons are not in this family and are reported separately. The adaptation family comprises 12 contrasts across ERM, output consistency, and CTC against augmentation for both heads and grammars. The direct frozen family compares the Rotary and 2F donor changes and the Rotary V and S effects for each grammar. The phase-restoration family contains two comparisons with full D. The equal-radius family has six V-versus-P contrasts over three heads and two grammars. Holm adjustment is applied within each family after the relevant block sets are complete. Complete unrounded effects, intervals, standardized paired effects dzd_{z}, and raw/adjusted pp values accompany the analysis record. The 95% bootstrap intervals apply to individual contrasts. Holm correction controls the comparison family, so its rejection threshold can differ.

With four blocks, even unanimous nonzero differences cannot give a two-sided exact p<0.125p<0.125. With eight, the minimum is 0.0078125. Cohen’s paired dzd_{z} is reported when the block-difference SD is positive, alongside uncertainty in percentage points.

A.6 Recovery-panel replay and composition controls

The recovery-panel replay contains 480 images per block per grammar. The first four blocks use cached earlier predictions and the other four are reconstructed with the same protocol. We hold the encoder, feature scaling, readouts, and decision threshold fixed. Paired effects weight blocks equally. The replay intervals resample blocks and, within block, connected components linking source and donor programs. Selection of the jointly exact subset is specific to each pair of views. It conditions on decoding outcomes. G5r donor effects are small where Rotary is close to chance. The 2F and GRU donor changes on G5c are −1.82-1.82 and −0.55-0.55 pp, respectively.

The G5c composition-control panel contains 960 archived source images, 120 per block. It preserves each queried tile and its position. The composition intervention changes surrounding nonidentity operation values while preserving their total increment modulo five and their identity positions. The permutation control preserves the operation multiset. Same-symbol rerendering changes local rendering draws without changing the surrounding symbols. Three draws are averaged per source for random controls and a single donor is used for the donor condition. All 316,212 query audits pass. The maximum anchor probability discrepancy is 0.00170, with no decision changes. Interval estimates resample the eight block means using 10,000 draws. The channel-panel matrix (Table A5) uses a different donor assignment and different perturbation definitions.

Two- and six-edit direction tests attain 50.87% (95% CI [48.78, 52.99]) and 51.98% ([49.38, 54.58]) ordering accuracy, below the 65% target. A separate five-candidate test uses 60 archived source images per block. Original-view endpoint accuracy is 79.38% ([75.63, 82.71]), below the 80% capability criterion. The fixed-sum result shows sensitivity to composition, although the internal rule is not identified. The composition-control and channel panels are stratified subsets of the recovery panel.

A.7 Training budgets and full-encoder controls

Table A6 lists the training and adaptation regimes.

At encoder LR 10−510^{-5}, the joint clean arm reaches 50.83% on F and 51.35% on D. Its mean selected validation BA is 51.61%, compared with 96.41% for the frozen-encoder arm. All 21.63M encoder parameters are trainable, with nonzero gradient checks at the patch projection and first and last attention blocks. At this validation accuracy, the small F-to-D gaps of the joint arms are not informative.

Before adaptation, the differentiable encoder and archived head achieve 96.25% on validation. Its validation BA matches the cached-feature score in all four blocks. The rate control keeps the head schedule fixed. Encoder LR 10−710^{-7} gives 96.98% validation BA, 87.92% on F, and 72.19% on D. Encoder LR 10−610^{-6} gives 98.12% validation BA, 88.23% on F, and 73.75% on D. Both rates preserve validation performance and retain a donor penalty in this adaptation regime.

Joint adaptation updates all DINOv2 parameters and the rotary head. Gradients are checked in the patch embedding and first and last attention blocks. The encoder learning rate is 10−510^{-5}, the head rate is 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, and batch size is 16. For paired training, one random queried feature is replaced by the feature from a donor canvas that preserves that tile. This keeps training tractable while evaluation uses a donor view for every queried node. All arms start from the existing checkpoints; Table A7 reports four blocks.

Under the original 5,040-update schedule, the G5c isolated Transformer and Mamba-1 heads reach 75.15% and 83.84%. They have 128,170 and 132,282 trainable parameters, respectively. Table A8 separates this architecture comparison from the earlier 512-update controls.

On the shared four-block context panel, G5c Transformer goes from 65.00% to 49.38%, and Mamba-1 goes from 61.56% to 55.21%. Table A9 reports paired effects and decision flips for the same 240 programs per block. G5r Transformer changes from 50.62% to 54.48% and flips 36.56% of decisions. The width-matched GRU retains high accuracy in both contexts.

The complete Mamba-1 comparison uses the validated implementation described above. The comparison measures capability at the recorded schedule and model sizes.

A.8 Training context versus test context

In the earlier G5c panel, neighboring operations are more decodable from full-context features than from isolated features (58.00% versus 23.58%). Metadata alone yields 23.49%. Yet training and testing Rotary with isolated features improves length extrapolation. An input-to-phase map can respond strongly to information from surrounding nodes that is unnecessary once the ordered local operations are supplied. The operation-value and phase interventions test this account within the fitted systems.

Removing context at inference produces a different result. The full-trained Rotary head drops from 89.27% to 50.57%, and fixed decoding with execution drops to 67.71% on those isolated views. The frozen models now receive a feature distribution they did not train on. The same transformation affects symbol recovery as well as learned computation. This distinction motivates testing adaptation with paired views while measuring performance on the original input.

The endpoint controls show why net accuracy and per-example sensitivity can differ. A previous endpoint probe ranks changes at 99.04%, while prefix exchange changes Rotary BA from 87.34% to 87.40%. There are 82 corrections and 80 new errors. The near-zero net change and the small state-tile effect argue against an explanation based only on endpoint leakage.

The identities below describe the implemented recurrences exactly and show how paired inputs enter the state and readout. and a positive sigmoid decay. Keys and queries are unit-normalized. The four matrix memories start at zero, and inactive padded steps leave them unchanged.

Index the nn encoded nodes from start to candidate endpoint. For any two input sequences, subtracting their affine recurrences yields

Writing the final two terms as EtE_{t} and substituting recursively proves the main text’s finite transport identity. No differentiability assumption is needed. Its norm bound follows from the triangle inequality and ‖X​A‖F≤‖X‖F​‖A‖2\|XA\|_{F}\leq\|X\|_{F}\|A\|_{2}. For a product of delta factors, each unit-key factor has eigenvalues 11 and 1−β1-\beta with β∈[0,2]\beta\in[0,2], so its spectral norm is at most one. Rotary has norm ρ\rho. Both 2F and Rotary are therefore nonexpansive, so the bound alone does not rank their robustness. The bound discards innovation directions and their cancellation. A large state distance can leave the decision unchanged, whereas a small distance can cross a boundary when the classification margin is small. This motivates a squared innovation penalty. Our normalized penalty differs from this unnormalized bound, and a changing query/readout requires additional terms to obtain a logit bound. The readout-aware extension below supplies explicit constants and measures bound tightness. The effect of minimizing these innovations is evaluated through task accuracy and paired decision stability.

Signed-margin decomposition.

For Rotary, use the hybrid transition At∗=ρtD​R​(θtF)A_{t}^{*}=\rho_{t}^{D}R(\theta_{t}^{F}). The three local terms are

Etθ\displaystyle E_{t}^{\theta} =St−1F​(AtD−At∗),\displaystyle=S_{t-1}^{F}(A_{t}^{D}-A_{t}^{*}), Etρ\displaystyle E_{t}^{\rho} =St−1F​(At∗−AtF),\displaystyle=S_{t-1}^{F}(A_{t}^{*}-A_{t}^{F}), (A14)
EtB\displaystyle E_{t}^{B} =BtD−BtF.\displaystyle=B_{t}^{D}-B_{t}^{F}. (A15)

Propagating each term through the remaining donor transitions gives three contributions whose sum equals SnD−SnFS_{n}^{D}-S_{n}^{F}. The norm of their sum can be smaller than the sum of their norms. An angle difference contributes in proportion to the stored state in its rotation plane. The contributions have directions, and later transitions can rotate and attenuate them. The accumulated difference therefore depends on direction and propagation as well as chain length. To decompose the final logit margin, evaluate the actual nonlinear readout after adding the three state contributions in a fixed order, then substitute the query and residual. Consecutive logit differences telescope. Individual terms depend on the substitution order, and a decision changes only when the signed margin crosses zero.
