|mD−mF|\displaystyle|m^{D}-m^{F}| ≤C,\displaystyle\leq C, (A24)
C\displaystyle C =Lm​(‖Wo‖2​LN​V+du)2+du2.\displaystyle=L_{m}\sqrt{\big(\|W_{o}\|_{2}L_{N}V+d_{u}\big)^{2}+d_{u}^{2}}. (A25)

If |mF|>C|m^{F}|>C, the two binary decisions agree. If the original decision is also correct, the donor decision is correct. This is a sufficient condition; its failure does not imply a changed or incorrect decision.

Proof.

For each head, the exact read difference is

Sn,hD​qn,hD−Sn,hF​qn,hF=δn,h​qn,hD+Sn,hF​(qn,hD−qn,hF).S_{n,h}^{D}q_{n,h}^{D}-S_{n,h}^{F}q_{n,h}^{F}=\delta_{n,h}q_{n,h}^{D}+S_{n,h}^{F}(q_{n,h}^{D}-q_{n,h}^{F}). (A26)

The triangle inequality, the memory transport bound, and the spectral norm bound for the second term give ‖rD−rF‖2≤QD​U+J\|r^{D}-r^{F}\|_{2}\leq Q_{D}U+J. Thus ‖oD−oF‖2≤‖Wo‖2​LN​V+du\|o^{D}-o^{F}\|_{2}\leq\|W_{o}\|_{2}L_{N}V+d_{u} and ‖zD−zF‖22=‖oD−oF‖22+du2\|z^{D}-z^{F}\|_{2}^{2}=\|o^{D}-o^{F}\|_{2}^{2}+d_{u}^{2}. The margin Lipschitz inequality proves Eq. (A25). A change of sign requires |mD−mF|≥|mF||m^{D}-m^{F}|\geq|m^{F}|, which proves the strict decision condition. No assumption about labels, correct decoding, training convergence, or the donor distribution is used.

Constants for the implemented head.

Write the classifier as f⁡(z)=W2​GELU⁡(W1​z+b1)+b2f(z)=W_{2}\operatorname{GELU}(W_{1}z+b_{1})+b_{2}. For the exact GELU used here, supx|GELU′⁡(x)|<1.13\sup_{x}|\operatorname{GELU}^{\prime}(x)|<1.13, so

Lm=1.13∥(W2)1,:−(W2)0,:∥2∥W1∥2L_{m}=1.13\,\|(W_{2})_{1,:}-(W_{2})_{0,:}\|_{2}\|W_{1}\|_{2} (A27)

is valid. LayerNorm with learned scale γ\gamma and numerical constant ϵN\epsilon_{N} has the global bound ‖γ‖∞/ϵN\|\gamma\|_{\infty}/\sqrt{\epsilon_{N}}. A tighter segment bound is

LN=‖γ‖∞ϵN+mins∈[0,1]⁡‖cF+s​Δ​c‖22/d,L_{N}=\frac{\|\gamma\|_{\infty}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{N}+\min_{s\in[0,1]}\|c_{F}+s\Delta c\|_{2}^{2}/d}}, (A28)

where cFc_{F} and Δ​c\Delta c are the mean-centered original read and read difference, and dd is the read dimension. The minimum is a scalar quadratic minimum, attained at s=clip[0,1](−cF⊤Δc/∥Δc∥22)s=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}(-c_{F}^{\top}\Delta c/\|\Delta c\|_{2}^{2}) when Δ​c≠0\Delta c\neq 0; when Δ​c=0\Delta c=0 the denominator is constant. The LayerNorm Jacobian norm is at most the reciprocal normalization denominator times ‖γ‖∞\|\gamma\|_{\infty}, which proves this bound along the segment. These constants are evaluated on observed pairs and are not a certificate against every possible image edit.

Numerical tightness of the bound.

On the retained 48-pair length-10 G5c fixture from block 1, the maximum elementwise transport reconstruction error is 1.2×10−61.2\times 10^{-6}. The median ratio of observed to bounded displacement is 0.2400.240 for memory, 0.04840.0484 for the final read, and 0.0005100.000510 for the margin bound in Eq. (A25). Even the segment-specific LayerNorm constant certifies none of the 48 pairs; using the exact observed read distance instead of VV also certifies none. The median bound is 1.54×1041.54\times 10^{4} logit units, versus an original absolute margin of 13.8713.87. The certificate is valid but vacuous on this fixture. It does, however, show which terms the decision depends on.

State and decision invariance under CTC.

If every Et=0E_{t}=0 and the initial memories agree, induction gives StD=StFS_{t}^{D}=S_{t}^{F} at every step. Transition–write cancellation can therefore preserve the state exactly; it is not intrinsically a failure. If the final queries and residuals also agree, the full decisions agree. In contrast, zero CTC alone does not imply equal decisions. At the affine readout interface, the scalar example SnF=SnD=1S_{n}^{F}=S_{n}^{D}=1, qnF=1q_{n}^{F}=1, qnD=−1q_{n}^{D}=-1, and margin m=Sn​qnm=S_{n}q_{n} has Et=0E_{t}=0 but opposite decisions. The implemented head additionally contains an unconstrained residual-to-classifier path. The scalar example illustrates the missing assumption, not a measurement on a fitted model. An example within the implemented architecture is also possible: set the value projection to zero so that both memories stay zero, and let the classifier use one coordinate of unu_{n}. Two input projections giving that coordinate opposite signs change the decision while every Et=0E_{t}=0. A two-unit GELU pair can implement this linear margin exactly because GELU⁡(x)−GELU⁡(−x)=x\operatorname{GELU}(x)-\operatorname{GELU}(-x)=x. This construction establishes a possible failure mode within the architecture; the fitted checkpoint’s errors require empirical diagnosis.

Normalization introduces a second qualification. For one chain, write ηt=‖St−1F‖F2+‖BtF‖F2+ϵ\eta_{t}=\|S_{t-1}^{F}\|_{F}^{2}+\|B_{t}^{F}\|_{F}^{2}+\epsilon and ℓCTC=n−1​∑t‖Et‖F2/ηt\ell_{\rm CTC}=n^{-1}\sum_{t}\|E_{t}\|_{F}^{2}/\eta_{t}. If ηt≤M\eta_{t}\leq M for every node, then

U≤(∑t[∏j>taj]2)1/2​M​n​ℓCTC.U\leq\left(\sum_{t}\left[\prod_{j>t}a_{j}\right]^{2}\right)^{1/2}\sqrt{Mn\ell_{\rm CTC}}. (A29)

For nonexpansive transitions this is at most n​M​ℓCTCn\sqrt{M\ell_{\rm CTC}}. Thus a small mean normalized penalty, without scale control, query/residual control, and an adequate decision margin, is not a robustness guarantee. This bound permits length-dependent worst cases; it does not predict monotonic empirical degradation.

A targeted training implication.

The readout condition motivates testing consistency of the actual final memory read r=Sn​qnr=S_{n}q_{n} together with unu_{n}, in addition to the paired task loss. This covers the query and residual terms omitted by CTC while allowing transition–write cancellation that preserves the computed state. The resulting readout consistency objective is a falsifiable training hypothesis. Its effect on accuracy requires comparison with ordinary augmentation and output consistency under matched tuning and compute, including the clean–donor trade-off. Because the proof is pair-specific, transfer to new donor mechanisms and longer chains remains an empirical question.

B.3 State-direction controls in 2F and GRU

We reuse the previously evaluated 1,920-row DINOv2 full-budget test, with fixed 2F and GRU checkpoints and no fitting. For 2F, hold the original final query and residual fixed and set Δ​r=(SD−SF)​qF\Delta r=(S^{D}-S^{F})q^{F}. The local projection p=∇rmF⋅Δ​rp=\nabla_{r}m^{F}\cdot\Delta r approximates the state-only margin change. The flip-ranking score is −sign⁡(mF)​(mF+p)-\operatorname{sign}(m^{F})(m^{F}+p): it combines the original margin with the projected change. Norm ranking uses relative state displacement within that head; original uncertainty uses −|mF|-|m^{F}|.

Table A10 compares decision-flip rankings with projection-error measurements.

For 2F, the projection has mean block Spearman correlation .765 with the exact state-only margin change, but its 4.83-logit average absolute error remains substantial. Curvature and the omitted query/residual changes make the combined score a paired association rather than a predictor of errors or repairs. GRU’s linear final classifier makes its projection an exact reconstruction of margin change up to numerical error, so its perfect flip ranking checks the algebra.

B.4 Recoverability and the learned decision

Let dd be a fixed role decoder and ℰ\mathcal{E} the exact executor. If every token is recovered, then ℰ⁡(d⁡(Z))\mathcal{E}(d(Z)) is correct. Its error event is therefore contained in the union of token errors, giving Pr⁡(rule error)≤∑tPr⁡(tokent​ error)\Pr(\text{rule error})\leq\sum_{t}\Pr(\text{token}_{t}\text{ error}). This implication is one-way: compensating start and endpoint mistakes can preserve legality. The decoder-executor accuracy is therefore a lower bound on what this interface can achieve.

A simple counterexample shows that recovery alone does not constrain the learned head. Let ZZ be the complete one-hot token sequence, so decoding is perfect. A learned function that always outputs the opposite of the correct answer has error one. The empirical value of the comparison is consequently the coexistence of a fixed successful decoding procedure and errors of a particular learned system under matched inputs. The channel interventions then ask how that system’s computation changes.

B.5 Numerical and channel checks

The diagnostic reconstructs each tested matrix head from its actual projection, convolution, normalized keys/queries, transition factors, writes, normalization, residual, and classifier. Its factual probability must agree with the archived head forward within 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. For every paired sequence, propagated innovations must reconstruct the state difference within 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} in maximum absolute element error; the norm bound must hold to that tolerance. The saved audit reports actual residuals, per-sequence bounds and the pass threshold.

Replacing AA, write BB, query qq, or residual uu alone defines different synthetic networks at inference time. Rotary phase and decay swaps separate the two factors in AA. Other channels stay original in those substitutions. In the reverse experiment only the original phase is restored within D. Both CPU replays are checked against the archived GPU predictions before restoring phase. For each of F and D, all decisions match at the threshold across 240 images per grammar and block, with two grammars and eight blocks. The cross-device tolerance is 10−410^{-4} on probability, and the within-device transport check retains 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. The swaps measure conditional responses; Table A11 gives the complete background–phase comparison. Interactions can prevent their BA changes from adding to the full donor effect. We also record feature distance, phase RMS, mean decay displacement, final-output CKA, state distance, local innovation norms and propagated upper bounds.

Phase replay and angular magnitude.

On the retained 48-program fixture, the candidate swap has the largest median single-node margin displacement, whereas restoration over all operation nodes repairs more new errors. On the two earlier fresh 384-pair panels, donor-phase replay ranks decision flips with mean block AUROCs .88 and .92, compared with .56 and .51 for angular RMS. These are paired, model-dependent scores that use both views. Seven of eight blocks in the 11-operation panel are below the 80% clean capability gate, so these rankings mainly describe low-capability models.

B.6 Same-example separation on the four-block panel

The earlier four-block 480-row G5c panel adds joint outcome counts. Its Rotary BA changes from 89.27% to 71.61% under D, while the rule interface changes from 96.61% to 96.88%. Of 417 newly incorrect Rotary answers, 388 have correct rule-interface answers in both contexts. The rule-stable set covers 1,817/1,920 examples and also contains 72 of 78 Rotary corrections. Table A12 gives the full accounting. These examples overlap with the eight-block panel and are reported separately; Fig. A2 illustrates actual paired decisions. The channel panel additionally counts exact recovery of every displayed token in both contexts by rerunning the fixed ridge decoder. We check its legality outputs against the previously archived answers.

Appendix C Training Controls and Generalization Boundaries

C.1 Matched head adaptation

The four adaptation arms start from the same original full-context checkpoint and fixed normalization, using the same 2,000 training and 480 validation rows. Donors are selected within each split to avoid leakage. ERM receives two original views, while the other arms receive original and donor views. Task and state losses are averaged across views. Output consistency measures squared Euclidean distance between the two class-probability vectors, and transport consistency uses the normalized local affine innovation. Both weights are fixed at 0.1 without a test-driven sweep.

All arms use batch 128, 256 updates, AdamW learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay, weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at one. The checkpoint maximizing the mean of clean and donor validation BA at 32-update intervals is retained, using the earliest maximum on ties. The ERM arm uses the same criterion. Table A13 reports all original and donor scores. The other pixel interventions are included in the source predictions. Runtime includes the additional penalty computation and is reported by arm.

Paired accuracy contrasts.

For G5c Rotary, the clean and donor changes of ordinary augmentation relative to ERM have 95% block-bootstrap intervals of [−5.68-5.68, −1.20-1.20] and [3.443.44, 7.197.19] pp, respectively. The clean change of CTC relative to augmentation is −0.68-0.68 pp ([−2.24-2.24, 0.520.52]). These are per-contrast intervals. For the donor gain of ordinary augmentation, the two-sided sign-flip pp is 0.0078 before adjustment and 0.0938 after Holm adjustment over the twelve donor contrasts. Figure A3 shows the observed trade-off and the paired effects relative to augmentation.

C.2 Angle consistency as a training objective

At a fixed step and memory, let S=St−1FS=S^{F}_{t-1}. Expanding the update difference gives

E=S⁡[ρD​(RD−RF)+(ρD−ρF)​RF]+BD−BF.E=S\big[\rho_{D}(R_{D}-R_{F})+(\rho_{D}-\rho_{F})R_{F}\big]+B_{D}-B_{F}. (A30)

The first term inside the brackets is exactly the transition difference between D and D with the original rotation restored. This decomposition uses the original trajectory state and attributes local differences at that state. It allows cancellation. For example, take S=e1​e1⊤S=e_{1}e_{1}^{\top} in two dimensions, RF=IR_{F}=I, RD=R⁡(π/2)R_{D}=R(\pi/2), and ρF=ρD=0.8\rho_{F}=\rho_{D}=0.8. Set BF=0B_{F}=0 and BD=−0.8​S​(RD−RF)B_{D}=-0.8S(R_{D}-R_{F}). The donor write has rank one and admits the rotary write parameterization. Then E=0E=0 despite a quarter-turn phase difference. This allowed update preserves the next state when the incoming states agree. If every innovation is zero from the common zero initialization, the entire states agree. Cancellation therefore does not explain a failure of state preservation; the example only shows that angle agreement is unnecessary. A small local innovation at one step does not erase differences accumulated earlier. Query and residual changes can still alter the final decision, as shown by the readout analysis.

For a planar rotation, tr⁡(RF⊤​RD)=2​cos⁡(θD−θF)\operatorname{tr}(R_{F}^{\top}R_{D})=2\cos(\theta_{D}-\theta_{F}) and ‖RF‖F2=‖RD‖F2=2\|R_{F}\|_{F}^{2}=\|R_{D}\|_{F}^{2}=2. Expanding ‖RD−RF‖F2\|R_{D}-R_{F}\|_{F}^{2} gives 4​[1−cos⁡(θD−θF)]4[1-\cos(\theta_{D}-\theta_{F})]. The term vanishes for angles a full turn apart. It controls the rotation independently of memory energy, decay, or writes. Supervised losses still determine which rotations are useful. A constant angle predictor would satisfy the angular penalty, so accuracy and sensitivity to genuine operation edits are necessary checks.

Prospective comparison.

Use paired augmentation as the main comparator, with output consistency and CTC as controls. Match the initial heads, training views, and updates. Choose regularizer weights on validation data under comparable tuning budgets. Lock independent test programs and their donor assignments before analysis. Report paired angular discrepancy and both original and donor BA, including whether clean long-chain performance meets a prespecified tolerance. Include a genuine edit to the queried operation that changes the correct answer as a control for task sensitivity. The operation-only mask applies to the training penalty. Frozen substitutions act on all valid nodes. The separate development screen below reports matched tests of this objective.

C.3 Full-encoder gradient and selection checks

The full-encoder control starts from the same pretrained DINOv2-S/14 weights and archived full-budget rotary checkpoint in every arm. Frozen and Joint use original views, while Joint+Augmentation and Joint+CTC create one random node-preserving donor canvas per training example. Only the corresponding queried feature is substituted into the original sequence. All auxiliary labels remain those of the original program. At evaluation, each queried feature is obtained from its own donor canvas, matching the node-wise diagnostic logic. Training and test donor assignments use a separate deterministic seed from the frozen factorial experiment.

The implementation obtains differentiable spatial patch features directly from the encoder with gradients enabled. It checks nonzero gradients in the patch projection and attention projections of the first and last transformer blocks. Every encoder parameter is trainable in the joint arms. AdamW uses encoder rate 10−510^{-5} and head rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, batch 16, 256 updates, cosine decay, and joint gradient clipping at one. Checkpoints are selected on clean validation BA every 64 updates, identically across arms.

C.4 Architecture and learning-rate sensitivity

The replay comparison uses the 240-row shared panel within blocks 1–4 for each grammar. For Transformer, Mamba-1, and the parameter-matched GRU, the selected checkpoint first reproduces archived probabilities on the original feature cache. It then receives the rerendered factorial features, using its fixed training normalization. Table A9 reports both absolute BA and within-block donor change for these same programs. The flip rate counts any original/donor decision disagreement, including both new errors and corrections. This matters when a low-accuracy model has a small mean BA change.

Low early validation scores under encoder LR 10−510^{-5} motivated the smaller-rate control. The eight additional runs keep the same initial weights, clean batches, head schedule, and eligible checkpoint steps. We trace validation BA and feature drift at steps 0, 8, 32, 64, 128, 192, and 256. The early observations describe the trajectory, while only multiples of 64 are eligible for checkpoint selection. Table A14 lists all rates. At step 8, the mean raw feature RMSE relative to initialization is 0.070 at 10−710^{-7} and 0.508 at 10−610^{-6}. This measures early representation drift in the two lower-rate arms. The original 10−510^{-5} run records validation from step 64.

Equal-radius feature directions.

Let v=ZV−ZFv=Z^{V}-Z^{F} and p=ZP−ZFp=Z^{P}-Z^{F} after the head’s fixed training normalization. For each program we take r=min⁡(‖v‖F,‖p‖F)r=\min(\|v\|_{F},\|p\|_{F}) over all valid nodes and replay ZF+r​v/‖v‖FZ^{F}+rv/\|v\|_{F} and ZF+r​p/‖p‖FZ^{F}+rp/\|p\|_{F}. A zero displacement produces the original features. Both interpolations stay between the original and perturbed vectors. They equalize aggregate displacement and can differ in the distribution of changes over nodes or coordinates. We check their achieved radii and original-context decision agreement. Because the interpolation takes place in feature space, this comparison concerns synthetic feature sequences.

C.5 Decoder choice and regularization

The additional G5c decoder audit uses blocks 1–4, a common cap of 12,000 training and 6,000 validation tokens per role, and original-context training-role normalization. Ridge regularization spans 10−510^{-5}, 10−310^{-3}, 0.1, 10 and 1000. Logistic regression and linear SVM choose C∈{0.01,1,100}C\in\{0.01,1,100\} on original validation accuracy. All ridge strengths are reported; selection uses original validation accuracy. The rules and role information are held fixed across decoder families. Table A15 shows accuracy for all decoder variants. The numerical retry increases the iteration cap from 1,000 to 10,000 and keeps the original samples and validation selection. All selected logistic and SVM fits converged in the numerical retry.

C.6 Longer computational streams

We additionally sample 240 fresh programs at each of 10, 20, 30, and 50 nonidentity operations, for both grammars and each of the eight trained blocks. This yields 15,360 streams. Each start, operation, and endpoint feature is sampled by its true role and symbol from the archived held-out isolated-token bank, with the exact source row and node retained. Correct endpoints are computed by the grammar. Balanced negative endpoints differ from that endpoint. The original isolated-trained heads and fixed isolated-trained decoders are reused without adaptation.

The test uses held-out DINOv2 features encoded in isolation. Their retained absolute pixel positions can vary nonmonotonically along the new sequence. The length-10 row controls for this changed construction before the longer streams test sequence computation. On G5c, Rotary scores 98.49% at 10 operations and 59.48% at 50. At 50 operations, the 2F head, GRU, and fixed rules reach 92.24%, 99.58%, and 98.65%. Fig. A4 includes the intermediate lengths and the order-sensitive grammar. The contrasting curves are evidence about computation on recomposed features.

C.7 Context dose, probes, and calibration

The earlier dose study retains the queried node plus radius k=0,1,2,4k=0,1,2,4, full context, or donor neighbors within radius two. Each cell uses the same short budget. On G5c, isolated and radius-two donor features yield nearly identical neighbor decoding (23.62% and 23.63%), but Rotary BA is 76.77% and 48.39%. Matched probe scores therefore coexist with sharply different task performance.

Neighbor probes include current-symbol, position, and node-count metadata. Full-context G5c features support mean BA 58.00% for offsets ±1\pm 1, versus 23.58% for isolated features and 23.49% for metadata alone. Endpoint change ranking uses 1,500 matched pairs per block. Prefix exchange uses a separate 240-pair subset. Its 82 corrections and 80 losses explain how a negligible net accuracy change can coexist with individual decision flips.

Validation-selected scalar thresholds change original full-context Rotary long-chain BA from 88.57% to 88.50%. A test-optimal scalar threshold, selected retrospectively as an oracle diagnostic, reaches only 89.07% on average. Full-budget original-width and parameter-matched isolated GRUs remain approximately 99.6% on both tasks. Table A16 lists the additional frozen-backbone controls; these use shared programs and a fixed projection to 384 input dimensions when required.

Appendix D Visual Vocabulary, Legends, and VLM Controls

D.1 Capability gates and scope

Table A17 lists the capability and transfer limits that bound the mechanism claims.

D.2 Vocabulary changes and legends

An unfamiliar glyph vocabulary changes the mapping from pixels to operation identities. A decoder trained on the original mapping has no way to recover a new one without extra information. The prior legend controls therefore distinguish an uninformative renaming from a labeled legend that specifies the intended mapping. The rule executor knows the grammar but cannot infer an unknown glyph mapping from the task label alone.

The legend audit includes independent 11-step programs, matched incorrect bindings, fixed feature/decoder/head checkpoints, and saved per-query predictions. These controls therefore test recovery under a supplied correspondence and supplied decoder role labels.

D.3 Bounded open-model comparisons

The prior comparison uses Qwen3-VL-2B [1] and SmolVLM2-500M [16], evaluated locally on the same 320 programs. Each model receives full images, ordered node tiles, or ground-truth symbolic text, with a common legend and transition table: 960 outputs per model, 1,920 total. The official scored protocol constrains a Yes/No single-token choice. Table A18 gives the results.

An early free-response trial allowed only eight generated tokens and often ended before producing a scorable answer. SmolVLM2’s default image splitting also produced 89 requests beyond its configured 8,192-token limit. The scored rerun disabled splitting. The near-chance results concern that constrained interface.

VLM capability.

These small models are near chance even on symbolic input, so their scores say little about visual context. A useful VLM test would first establish execution on symbolic input and on ordered tiles, and only then apply a label-preserving context intervention to full canvases. The structured follow-up in Sec. D.4 uses a separate model, parser and program panel; it yields six wrong decisions among 58 exactly transcribed full-canvas chains (Table A19).

D.4 Structured multimodal follow-up

We evaluate the model identified as Claude Sonnet 4.6 by the AICodeMirror API on 64 archived hue-carrier programs. The sample contains two programs per grammar, length (3 or 10 nonidentity operations), block (1–4), and legality label. Each program is presented as its full canvas, as an ordered strip of indexed node crops, and as ground-truth symbols. The two visual conditions include the same labeled legend. All three conditions supply the transition table, order and candidate convention. Input layouts and token counts differ. We use temperature zero and a 1,536-token output cap, and request the start, all operation IDs including identities, candidate, complete state trajectory, and binary decision. A separate four-program pilot fixed the JSON parser and output cap before testing. We accept one complete JSON object, including a final fenced object after prose. One symbolic request failed and counts as incorrect. No returned response hit the token cap.

On full canvases, 6 of 58 exactly reported chains receive an incorrect model decision, and 20 of those 58 have an incorrect reported trajectory. On true-symbol input the corresponding counts are 15 and 29 of 63 parsed cases. All parsed cases with both an exact chain and an exact trajectory yield a correct decision. Model decisions can be right despite an earlier state error, as in the long G5r full-canvas cell. The exact executor changes the evaluation question: for example, it scores 62/64 on the full-canvas transcriptions while the model itself scores 56/64. It evaluates transcribed symbols using the supplied exact execution algorithm. Moving from the canvas to tiles fixes five model decisions and breaks twelve; moving from the canvas to symbols fixes six and breaks fourteen. These results come from one model on a small fixed panel. Raw requests, responses and scoring code are saved with the release.

VSTAT [22] emphasizes continuous event perception and visual integration in videos, while MET-Bench [5] compares visual and textual entity-state reasoning. Both benchmarks offer settings for testing the recoverability/execution distinction beyond the current generated-symbol tasks. Realistic traversal, ambiguous symbols, natural scene clutter, and unknown transition rules are left for future work.

Appendix E Independent Programs and Development Screens

E.1 Separate recognition and execution tests

Given an ordered list of queries, pair the original and changed views before scoring. The following evaluation uses a role-specific classifier and exact transition rules.

  1. 1.

    Replace the surroundings for each query and keep that tile’s pixels and position. Encode and concatenate the queried features in the supplied order.

  2. 2.

    Decode the start, each operation, and the proposed endpoint. Execute the decoded program. Run the same executor with true tokens as a separate oracle.

  3. 3.

    Score the fitted head in both contexts. Count paired decision changes over all programs, then describe changes among pairs with both chains exact.

  4. 4.

    Recompute the head twice with exchanged phases. Use donor angles with original decay, writes, query and residual, then original angles with the corresponding donor channels.

E.2 Frozen mechanism on disjoint families

The new G5c panels each contain 48 programs per block, one legal and one illegal endpoint for each of 24 canonical families, across eight blocks. We exclude all previously used families of the same length, canonicalized under operation renaming and reversal. A cyclic donor assignment deranges entire families within each block, matching the source label and keeping the query tile fixed. The 11-operation panel was specified first. Its capability gate was 80% original BA per block. We then tested a separately generated 10-operation panel with one identity to match the original long-chain regime and keep the node count fixed. This follow-up changes both the number of operations and the presence of an identity.

Table A20 and Fig. A5 compare frozen interventions on the disjoint-family panels.

The original BA in the 11-operation panel ranges from 47.92% to 81.25%. Seven of the eight blocks fall below the capability gate. The panel therefore misses the prespecified mechanism criterion. Holm-adjusted two-sided sign-flip probabilities for the three effects in table order are 0.156, 0.094 and 0.281. Of 83 new donor errors, 66 occur with both decoded chains exact. The 10-operation follow-up has original BA 68.75–93.75% across blocks. The maximum elementwise state reconstruction residual is 1.7×10−61.7\times 10^{-6}. Across these blocks, the median ratio of the net state displacement to the sum of the three component norms ranges from 0.63 to 0.69. The within-block correlation between angular RMS and the change in signed true-class margin ranges from −0.25-0.25 to 0.140.14. The signs and magnitudes depend on the original state and on subsequent transitions. Both panels have fixed lengths within block.

E.3 Transfer across state carriers and operation glyphs

Table A21 gives both blocks for each renderer and grammar. The external two-block program sets use 11 nonidentity operations. They reuse each underlying program across the familiar rendering, a hue carrier, and two new operation glyph inventories. Each new glyph renderer changes the symbol inventory while the paired original-versus-donor test keeps the current queried glyph identical. The visual changes across renderers can lower original performance, and the two blocks provide a range of observations.

E.4 Matched-budget training on disjoint programs

Figure A6 compares every trained objective with matched augmentation on the independent test. We use the same initialization and sample order for each arm, with 80 training and 80 validation rows per block, two supervised forwards per update, batch size 32, and 64 AdamW updates. The validation criterion weights original and donor BA equally. Clean ERM, paired augmentation, output consistency, CTC and operation-node phase consistency are compared on the first two development blocks. In the phase penalty, the original-view angle supplies a stop-gradient target. The independent test compares phase consistency with augmentation on the 10-operation families in all eight blocks. The prespecified gates require a donor benefit of at least 2 points and an original penalty smaller than 1 point, using the respective lower confidence bounds.

Relative to augmentation, phase consistency changes original BA by 0.520.52 [0.000.00, 1.561.56] pp and donor BA by −0.52-0.52 [−1.30-1.30, 0.000.00] pp. The joint criterion fails because the donor-gain lower bound does not reach +2+2 pp; the clean-capability requirement is met. The mean paired operation-angle RMS change is −0.0057-0.0057 radians.

E.5 Frozen locality and symbol interfaces

A budget-matched visibility screen keeps the queried tile and either the two nearest or the two farthest tiles in their original positions. Both interventions use the same canvas, encoder, frozen heads, and number of visual forwards. The held-out clean-source Rotary BA in the near condition is 60.42% and 54.17% in the two development blocks, versus 89.58% in the full original condition in each block. The far comparison scores 52.08% and 54.17%. The substantial absolute loss disqualifies this frozen masking method under the clean-accuracy gate.

Role-specific ridge decoders learned from the small development split use the same frozen features, with training on originals or matched original/donor pairs. The decoder-executor and learned recurrence can fail on different examples. The executor given true symbols obtains 100% in the closed grammar. In a separate glyph transfer pilot, supervised decoding on one glyph inventory yields incomplete chains on unseen glyph assignments, even when the original grammar and executor are unchanged. All fits and per-condition recognition and decision scores are recorded with the experiment data.

In a secondary transfer screen, the two development checkpoint pairs yield donor gains from −0.56-0.56 to 2.082.08 pp across the 11-operation and alternate-renderer conditions.

Operation-node phase consistency.

For paired views, average over valid operation nodes tt (including identities) and rotation planes jj:

ℒθ=𝔼i,t,j​[1−cos⁡(θi,t,jF−θi,t,jD)].\mathcal{L}_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{i,t,j}\left[1-\cos(\theta^{F}_{i,t,j}-\theta^{D}_{i,t,j})\right].

The original angle is a stop-gradient target. In one plane the squared Frobenius distance between the rotations is four times the corresponding term. In two development blocks, phase consistency and matched augmentation yield identical original and donor BA, while operation-node phase RMS is lower by 0.012 and 0.001 radians. The independent eight-block test uses the selected training objective and the same matched augmentation baseline.

Both chains exact in the eight-block tests.

In the 11-operation panel, 283 of 384 pairs meet joint exactness. Donor minus original BA is −11.41-11.41 pp [−19.63-19.63, −3.01-3.01], donor-phase injection is −9.85-9.85 pp [−17.47-17.47, −3.12-3.12], and restoration is +6.48+6.48 pp [−1.29-1.29, 14.0814.08]. Restoration corrects 45 of 66 new errors in that subset, and 48 of 283 decisions still differ from the original. In the 10-operation-plus-identity follow-up, 305 of 384 pairs meet joint exactness. The corresponding contrasts are −16.14-16.14 pp [−24.54-24.54, −8.06-8.06], −15.85-15.85 pp [−24.35-24.35, −8.30-8.30], and +18.38+18.38 pp [10.7810.78, 25.0425.04]. Restoration corrects 63 of 77 new errors, and 46 of 305 decisions differ from the original. These intervals resample whole blocks.

E.6 Target-renderer refit

We train a separate Rotary head in each target operation-glyph renderer, initialized from its archived familiar-renderer checkpoint. DINOv2 and feature standardization are fixed. Each fit uses 80 clean training rows and 80 clean validation rows, sampled by label from the formal program split, with canonical families excluded between fitting, validation, and testing. AdamW runs for 64 updates at batch size 32, with initial learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, cosine decay, and gradient clipping at 1. We select the earliest checkpoint with maximal validation BA among updates 16, 32, 48 and 64. The role decoder is independently fitted on the same 80 clean rows. The 11-operation test uses the independent glyph validation manifest; the 10-operation-plus-identity test uses blocks 1 and 2 of the length-matched follow-up. Both renderers share programs and donor identities within a block and length. States and identity tiles use the shared renderer.

Every zero-shot and refit block falls below the 80% original-BA gate (Tables A22 and A23). The selected refits reach 86.25–97.50% training BA but 45.00–55.00% validation BA. Original BA is 48.33–50.56% on the 11-operation tests and 41.67–52.08% on the length-matched tests. These observations localize a failure of generalization under this refit budget even within the target renderer. The fixed zero-shot probe recovers no complete chains jointly. The refitted probe identifies 99.3–100% of operations while start and endpoint recognition span 13.33–64.58% and 27.78–56.25%, respectively. It recovers both complete chains for only 1–23 programs per block. High operation recognition therefore coexists with poor full-chain recovery. The exact-subset estimates have small and sometimes single-label denominators. Phase substitutions change decisions, but with clean scores this low and few complete chains we draw no mechanism conclusion. Decay, write, query and residual controls in both directions and their per-block scores are in renderer_refit_by_block.csv.

E.7 Endpoint substitutions and frozen repair on new families

The start-only, candidate-only and joint truth replacements operate at the symbol interface. The original mixed-carrier role probes supply unchanged operations. We retain the exact grammar and labels for every arm. The all-true arm verifies agreement with the manifest labels. For the learned head, endpoint classes index the mean standardized visual feature of that class and role in orientation-carrier training rows. This is a feature intervention with a class-conditioned proxy. The last-operation auxiliary state classifier supplies a separate diagnostic. We compare its predicted state with the true candidate and verify that replacing the later candidate feature leaves the earlier prediction invariant.

We screen two deployable symbolic repairs on the eight development cells: an orientation-only ridge fit and a template reader for the two endpoint tiles with the operation decoder unchanged. Their original BA means are 52.34% and 99.31%, respectively. The template reader uses five existing legend exemplars per state and only the queried crop. For learned Rotary, we compare the frozen and target-renderer-refitted heads under the same local reader and class-prototype input. Their original BA means are 47.14% and 49.31%. We lock the highest-scoring arm in each path before constructing the new holdout. No holdout score changes the frozen selection.

The prospective panels use eight new program/render-seed blocks per renderer and length, with 48 pairs in each block. Every block has 24 new canonical families and two endpoint variants per family. Original and donor queries share pixels, position, and traversal. Glyph renderers share the underlying programs and donor assignments. Two calibration dictionaries and checkpoints alternate across blocks. The intervals describe variation across the independent program blocks conditional on these two calibrations. The learned-head mechanism gate requires at least 80% original BA in every block of a renderer-length panel. The symbolic executor is scored separately. In the repaired joint-exact subset, the rule path yields 100% BA in both views by construction. The Rotary path still averages 47.80–49.41% original BA across the four panels. Counts range from 356 to 383 of 384 pairs. Per-example predictions, flips and block intervals accompany the package.

Table A24 separates endpoint substitutions from complete-program execution on the same fresh pairs.

E.8 Operation-prefix interventions

The operation follow-up keeps the endpoint repair fixed. In each original and donor view, the local pixel reader supplies endpoint IDs and the fitted role probe supplies operation IDs. For a prefix of length kk, we replace the first kk operation features with standardized class centroids from calibration training. The matched pair of arms indexes the same centroids by either true or decoded IDs. The feature intervention changes the inputs at the same positions in both arms. In the separate symbolic path we use the same ID substitutions with the exact G5c executor. The identity counts as a displayed operation in both analyses. We check that an additional edit leaves the preceding auxiliary state logits invariant up to floating-point tolerance.

A true-ID class mean replaces an individual symbol observation with a calibration prototype. Replacing individual features by calibration means changes feature variance, cross-node correlations and potentially the distribution expected by the frozen recurrence. The true-versus-decoded comparison controls the ID used to select the same means, while retaining this distribution shift. Prototype-fed heads therefore test the substituted interface rather than the original-input mechanism.

We record the five-state prediction after the start and after every operation. At the last operation, we compare this prediction with the locally read candidate to form a separate legality estimate. Rotary’s native legality uses its candidate-position output and residual after the candidate update. The state-based decision therefore bypasses the candidate update and native classifier together. We fit calibration-only ridge readouts of the projected per-step output, its recurrent read component, the input residual, and the flattened post-update memory matrix. These probes test whether the correct state is accessible to the chosen readouts. Poor probe scores leave open whether a richer readout could recover the state.

Development compares the existing endpoint-only head, the same head given decoded operation prototypes, and a head refit on decoded prototypes for 64 additional AdamW updates on the 80 calibration training examples. The equal-cell original BA values are 49.31%, 53.30%, and 51.79%, respectively. We select the second path and freeze the selection, training inputs, and weights. The operation counterfactuals on previously evaluated endpoint pairs are kept separate from the prospective test. On the latter, each of eight new blocks per length uses eight new canonical families and two endpoint variants per family. We evaluate 11 operations before the length-matched 10 operations plus identity. The two renderers share program and donor assignments. Block intervals are conditional on the two alternating calibration dictionaries and checkpoint sets. Phase swaps are eligible only when the selected learned path reaches 80% original BA in all eight fresh blocks of its renderer-length panel.

Table A25 gives the operation-prefix interventions for every renderer–length panel.

Figure A7 compares the renderer capability gate and the state-tracking responses after endpoint and operation repair.

Across the 512 fresh pairs, the frozen operation probe reads 5,627/5,632 operation IDs in original views and 5,628/5,632 in donor views. Full true-ID replacement changes the learned decision in one original and three donor views relative to matched decoded-ID prototypes. The exact executor with true operations and local endpoints reaches 100% BA. The frozen learned arm scores 51.95% original and 52.73% donor BA, averaged across the four panels. The all-true prototype arm scores 52.15% in both views. For the selected non-oracle arm, the class prototype sequences are identical across views in 503 of 512 pairs, including all 16 pairs in the single high-scoring strokes block. This bottleneck collapses most of the original/donor feature variation.

For the non-oracle selected arm, the original-view last-state accuracies of the calibration-only probes of the projected output, recurrent read component, residual, and matrix memory are 23.24%, 24.41%, 14.45%, and 19.53%. Their state-equality BA values are 48.63%, 50.00%, 44.73%, and 52.34%. These are short-training to long-test readout results. In the true-operation arm, directly comparing the auxiliary last state to the local candidate yields 50.98% BA. The candidate-update and legality-readout stages can disagree with this comparison even when the auxiliary state is correct.

For the original-view all-true operation-prototype arm, auxiliary state accuracy is 72.66% at the start and 19.92% after the first operation. The matched decoded-ID arm has the same two means. With no operation replacement, first-operation accuracy is also low (20.70%). These values average the four renderer–length cells within each of eight program blocks; the four cells share the same blocks. First-operation accuracy is similarly low with and without replacement.

Appendix F Additional Replays and Audits

F.1 Exact patch support and one-canvas controls

DINOv2 receives the original 112×448112\times 448 array without a canvas resize. With 14-pixel patches and bilinear sampling, the horizontal patch coordinate at x=32+32​tx=32+32t is x/14−1/2x/14-1/2. The two adjacent columns and rows have positive interpolation weights. The exact initial pixel footprint is the corresponding 28×2828\times 28 rectangle. Its vertical range is [42,70)[42,70) and its horizontal range is [14​⌊x/14−1/2⌋,14​(⌊x/14−1/2⌋+2))[14\lfloor x/14-1/2\rfloor,14(\lfloor x/14-1/2\rfloor+2)). A nominal tile can miss up to four columns of this rectangle. We reconstruct the archived renders and paste back every pixel in the rectangle after the original tile paste. This preserves the query’s initial patch support and removes dependence on extrapolating the geometric result to encoder outputs.

RGB and donor audits.

The full revised panel has 24,333 G5c and 24,301 G5r query footprints. The ordinary donor changes at least one RGB pixel in 11,326 (46.55%) and 11,329 (46.62%) footprints, respectively. There are seven G5c and five G5r self-donors in 1,920 source programs per grammar. We keep them in the audits. Donor legality agrees with source legality in 950/1,920 G5c and 974/1,920 G5r programs. The G5c composite seen at an individual query is legal for 2,506/12,159 queries with legal source and 2,495/12,174 with illegal source. The respective G5r counts are 2,719/12,148 and 2,502/12,153. These counts are clustered within programs. They distinguish the label of the visible composite from the source label used by the evaluation.

All 1,536 clean and ordinary-donor decision anchors match the archive across both grammars and three heads. The maximum absolute probability difference is 0.02521. Guarded and common-canvas arms preserve initial sampled embeddings within 10−610^{-6}, despite differences after the first attention block. In G5c, guarded BA is 71.88% for Rotary, 95.31% for 2F and 97.66% for GRU. In G5r, it is 53.13%, 97.66% and 99.22%. The eight-block bootstrap keeps all examples from one block together. With the G5c Rotary head the original scores 89.06%, source duplication 65.63% and donor addition 56.25%. Donor addition versus source duplication is −9.38-9.38 pp ([−17.97,−0.78][-17.97,-0.78]). F.2 Sensitivity of the renderer capability gate

We prespecified 80% original BA in every block to require a clear margin over binary chance and avoid phase interpretation for weak learned arms. This is a design criterion rather than a hypothesis-test threshold. On the frozen operation repair, lowering the gate to 60% still leaves only 2/8, 3/8, 2/8 and 2/8 passing blocks across the four renderer-length panels. At 70, 80 and 90% the corresponding counts are 0/8, 0/8, 1/8 and 0/8. Thus no renderer-length panel passes an all-block criterion at any of these thresholds. We also record start and candidate confusion matrices stratified by view, renderer and length.

F.3 Validation-selected consistency follow-up

We test whether the local transport objective improves accuracy, and whether also constraining the query and residual paths helps. This follow-up uses a smaller data budget than the earlier 2,000-training-row, 480-validation-row, 256-update experiment (batch size 128). Eight frozen G5c Rotary heads are initialized from their archived checkpoints; each is adapted on 80 training and 80 validation rows using 64 updates, batch size 32, AdamW (×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4} initial learning rate, cosine decay, weight decay 0.01), and gradient clipping at 1. All arms share initialization and minibatch draws within a block. We compare clean continuation, ordinary two-view augmentation, probability consistency, binary-margin consistency, CTC, and readout transport consistency (RTC). The task loss is the legality cross-entropy plus 0.5 times the supervised state cross-entropy. Let 𝐳v\mathbf{z}^{v} be the binary logits, mv=z1v−z0vm^{v}=z^{v}_{1}-z^{v}_{0}, rv=vec⁡(STv​qTv)r^{v}=\operatorname{vec}(S_{T}^{v}q_{T}^{v}), and uv=uTvu^{v}=u_{T}^{v} for view v∈{F,D}v\in\{F,D\}. The added penalties are

ℒprob\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prob}} =𝔼​‖softmax⁡(𝐳D)−softmax⁡(𝐳F)‖22,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\|\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}^{D})-\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}^{F})\|_{2}^{2}, (A31)
ℒmargin\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{margin}} =𝔼​(mD−mF)2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}(m^{D}-m^{F})^{2}, (A32)
ℒRTC\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RTC}} =12​𝔼​[‖rD−rF‖22sg⁡(‖rF‖22)+ϵ+‖uD−uF‖22sg⁡(‖uF‖22)+ϵ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\|r^{D}-r^{F}\|_{2}^{2}}{\operatorname{sg}(\|r^{F}\|_{2}^{2})+\epsilon}+\frac{\|u^{D}-u^{F}\|_{2}^{2}}{\operatorname{sg}(\|u^{F}\|_{2}^{2})+\epsilon}\right], (A33)

where ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4} and sg\operatorname{sg} stops the gradient. Gradients pass through both view trajectories in the numerators. Each penalty is added with weight λ\lambda to the average task loss across the two views. RTC covers the actual pre-normalization readout and residual paths identified by the bound; it permits state-preserving transition/write cancellation. The comparison tests whether this broader objective improves accuracy. We evaluate λ∈{0.01,0.1,1}\lambda\in\{0.01,0.1,1\} for every consistency objective. A checkpoint maximizes the mean of original/donor validation balanced accuracy, checked every 16 updates; one weight per objective maximizes mean validation performance across the eight blocks, with ties favoring the smaller weight. All four objectives select λ=0.01\lambda=0.01. Checkpoints and weights are locked before generating the test. The adaptation cache has no shared base keys or exact programs between training and validation; 12–21 broader reversal/renaming canonical families overlap per block. The subsequent test contains 384 balanced rows from 192 globally distinct canonical families, excluded from all previously recorded panels. Each program has 10 nonidentity operations plus one identity. The same random derangement of donor families is evaluated with donor endpoint labels either preserved or reversed. These two conditions stratify a mixed-label donor rule under the per-query pixel-compositing protocol. Paired 95% percentile intervals resample the eight blocks 40,000 times. Unselected weights are evaluated after selection, with checkpoints and selected weights fixed. Table A26 gives accuracy contrasts for the selected weights, with the remaining weight responses in Fig. A9.

The fresh clean accuracy of the frozen head is 78.13%, and every selected adaptation arm reduces it. CTC gains 0.78 pp on label-preserving donors (95% CI [0.00,1.82][0.00,1.82]), and RTC gains 0.26 pp ([0.00,0.78][0.00,0.78]); exact two-sided sign-flip tests of the eight paired block effects give p=0.50p=0.50 and p=1.00p=1.00, respectively (all 282^{8} assignments, assuming sign-exchangeability under the null). On reversed-label donors, both mean differences are 0.00 pp; RTC has interval [−0.78,0.78][-0.78,0.78]. Against margin consistency, RTC gives +1.56+1.56 pp [−1.82,5.47][-1.82,5.47]. Neither objective gives a clear gain at the tested weights and budget.

Table A27 reports the measured training costs. RTC uses four recurrent trajectories per update versus two for ordinary augmentation. The 128-update augmentation control approximately matches the recurrent-trajectory count of 64-update RTC, and took 9.46 s/block versus 8.30 s/block for RTC. Task/state losses, readout computations and validation frequency differ, so FLOP counts can differ. All 120 adaptation fits took 701.1 s. Each 128-update control has eight checkpoint evaluations, while a 64-update fit has four. Against this control, CTC and RTC have donor differences of +1.82+1.82 pp [0.00,3.65][0.00,3.65] and +1.30+1.30 pp [0.00,2.60][0.00,2.60]. F.7 Phase substitutions by program role

In each panel and encoder we evaluate eight fixed blocks of 240 G5c programs. We exchange phase between the two views at operation nodes, the true last candidate, or both. Operation nodes include identities, and the candidate index uses each program’s length. Decay, write, query and residual use the base view. The start phase acts on zero initial memory, and exchanging it leaves the read and logits exactly unchanged. The factual replay agrees with the archived forward within 1.47×10−51.47\times 10^{-5} in probability, and the expanded final read agrees within 2.15×10−62.15\times 10^{-6}. Neither check changes a factual decision.

Table A32 gives both substitution directions on the channel panel and on previously evaluated held-out programs. We use 40,000 paired whole-block bootstrap draws and report unadjusted intervals. On the previously evaluated DINOv2 panel, restoring both roles achieves 76.82% BA and fixes 350 of 447 new errors, compared with 78.23% and 351 repairs for operation-only restoration. The added candidate substitution can introduce errors as well as correct them. A role intervention over all operation nodes measures their joint effect, while the individual-node fixture in Fig. A14 measures absolute margin displacement at one node.

For the candidate, we also exchange the query qnq_{n}, write BnB_{n} or residual unu_{n} using a fixed base prefix. The residual substitution changes both its addition to the read and its separate classifier input. Each has a smaller average recovery effect than operation-phase restoration. The phase–write interaction at the candidate is zero at the raw read to numerical precision (3.81×10−63.81\times 10^{-6} maximum absolute difference in the four-cell contrast), as expected from the sum of the two terms in the read. Interactions can appear after normalization and classification. The fixed prefix can already contain information about the candidate through global encoding. The archived arm and factorial tables report these interventions for both directions and for the jointly exact subsets.

F.8 Consistency objectives and margins on adaptation splits

We reevaluate saved checkpoints on every adaptation training and validation row, with both original and donor views. These short programs contain three to seven nonidentity operations. The eight blocks total 16,000 adaptation training and 3,840 validation rows. The validation rows previously selected checkpoints and weights. We keep the locked weights and use 40,000 whole-block bootstrap draws for intervals. Table A33 reports donor cross-entropies and the paired objective computed over both views. The CTC mean weights valid nodes and the RTC mean weights rows.

CTC reduces its penalty by 5.66% on training and 5.46% on validation. In training, augmentation makes 74 donor errors. CTC corrects 32 and introduces four, with one block contributing 31 of the net 28 additional correct predictions. On validation, CTC corrects 17 and introduces 14. RTC lowers its penalty by 2.71% and 2.06% on training and validation, respectively. RTC training BA falls by 0.3250.325 pp ([−0.875,−0.025][-0.875,-0.025]). Of the 274 augmentation validation errors, 232 have absolute true-label margins of at least one. In the 103 validation rows with smaller absolute margins, CTC introduces 13 errors and corrects 10. This split-level audit distinguishes objective and cross-entropy gains from changes in classification. The recorded checkpoints were selected separately, so their comparison combines the effects of the penalty, optimization and checkpoint selection.

Appendix G Confirmation on New Program Families

We generated this panel after the diagnostic results reported elsewhere in this document were known. It uses new canonical program families, while retaining the eight existing full-budget DINOv1 Rotary heads and their fixed role decoders. It is separate from the 1,920-pair channel panel and from the 11-operation and 10+110+1 panels of Sec. E. The protocol, model files, code, source inventory, exclusion union and eight input manifests were hashed and locked before encoding or scoring any new program. There is no new training, checkpoint selection or threshold tuning.

New families and the fixed donor law.

Each of eight blocks contains 24 new canonical families, each with a legal and an illegal endpoint: 384 program rows from 192 globally distinct families. Every program has ten nonidentity operations and exactly one identity, hence 13 nodes. Canonicalization removes identities, normalizes operation names by first occurrence, and takes the minimum of the forward and reversed normalized sequences. Cyclic rotations retain distinct canonical keys. We exclude displayed and source/negative families from all earlier training, validation and test row containers, the eight full original G5c manifests and the earlier canonical exclusions. An independent pre-result audit found no overlap with the locked exclusion union and no duplicate new family across blocks. Length eight had no available family under these exclusions, and length nine had only 174, fewer than the 192 required; length ten was chosen on this availability check, without model outcomes.

Both carriers are balanced within block. Donors follow the original row-level cyclic-shuffle law within split, node count, carrier and vocabulary. No row is its own donor. Thirteen of the 384 donor assignments use the opposite-endpoint sibling from the same canonical family; we kept them as assigned (Sec. G.1). The donor law operates at row level and permits these within-family assignments. At each query we preserve the source’s full-height 32-pixel tile and position in the donor canvas, encode separately, then assemble features in the supplied order. No new row is selected based on recognition or model accuracy.

Anchors and capability.

Before new encoding, 48 fixed source RGB anchors match byte-for-byte and 16 archived numerical anchors have no classification disagreement; their maximum probability discrepancy is 1.99×10−91.99\times 10^{-9}, below the locked 10−510^{-5} tolerance. MPS was used without invoking the predefined CPU fallback. All 4,992 new query-pixel checks pass, and the maximum sampled initial patch-embedding difference is zero. The factual phase replay satisfies its locked 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} probability tolerance and preserves factual decisions. Original BA ranges from 95.83% to 100%, so all eight blocks exceed the 80% interpretation gate.

Paired execution and restoration.

All 384 complete chains decode exactly in both views, so the jointly exact analysis coincides with the all-row analysis. Original and donor BA are 99.22% and 92.19%, a paired change of −7.03-7.03 pp (95% block-bootstrap interval [−11.46,−2.60][-11.46,-2.60]). There are 29 new donor errors, two donor corrections and 31 original/donor disagreements. Donor-phase injection lowers original BA to 92.97%. Restoring original phase raises donor BA to 98.70%, correcting 28 of the 29 new donor errors, while introducing three errors relative to donor predictions. Two of 384 predictions still differ from the original (99.48% agreement). Thus this new-program result supports a phase-sensitive execution pathway in the capable frozen G5c model, while retaining the distinction between repairing new errors and recovering all original predictions.

Table A34 reports both phase-exchange directions; Table A35 compares repair benefits with introduced errors and residual disagreement.

Operation-only restoration has the same aggregate results as full phase restoration; candidate-only restoration fixes one new donor error. All substitutions keep the recipient’s other channels and use both views as a diagnostic reference. This confirmation tests new program families with the fixed encoder, known vocabulary, supplied traversal and previously selected model family.

G.1 Sensitivity to within-family donors

Thirteen donor assignments in the 384-row confirmation use an opposite-endpoint sibling from the same canonical family. We retain the prespecified all-row estimate and additionally remove exactly these rows, with no re-encoding, refitting or donor reassignment. The sensitivity subset has 371 rows. Since deletion can unbalance labels, each block’s BA is recomputed as the mean of its classwise recalls before averaging the eight blocks equally. Intervals use 40,000 paired whole-block percentile resamples with seed 2026111011. This post hoc check uses the same frozen outputs. Table A36 reports the recomputed classwise scores and paired contrasts.

Appendix H Operation Phase from Local Pixels

In a two-block DINOv1 validation pilot we replace the operation-node phase projection with a small CNN. Both CNN variants use a 96×9696\times 96 RGB window at the supplied query center, the same architecture, initialization and fixed channel normalization. The local arm sets the exterior of the central 32×3232\times 32 tile to white. The context arm retains the surrounding pixels with white padding at image boundaries. Both CNNs supply all operation angles, including at identities. Start and candidate angles, decay, writes, queries and residuals still use the global features. The original Rotary head is retrained as a third arm. All fits use the same 16,000 training rows, common head initialization, batch sequence, 5,040 updates and task supervision. Checkpoint selection uses original-view BA on 6,000 validation rows. The balanced 480-row paired subset of that split is used for the donor diagnostic. The pilot ends at validation.

All 6,859 tested operation crops are byte-identical within pairs. The local angle differences are exactly zero in every recorded epoch in both blocks. On these queries the operation innovation becomes

Et=St−1F​(ρtD−ρtF)​R​(θt)+(BtD−BtF).E_{t}=S_{t-1}^{F}(\rho_{t}^{D}-\rho_{t}^{F})R(\theta_{t})+(B_{t}^{D}-B_{t}^{F}).

Equal angles remove one term in the transition difference, while decay and writes can still contribute to the state difference. To test reliance on input-varying operation angles, we replace each operation angle with the per-plane pooled circular mean of the original validation angles and apply it to both views. Original BA on the 480-row subset drops from 97.708% to 48.125% and from 100% to 52.083%. Donor BA changes from 65.208% to 50.417% and from 98.125% to 51.667%. The intervention uses no labels to compute the mean and makes no change to weights or checkpoint selection.

The local CNN retains higher donor BA than the context CNN on both blocks and lower donor BA than the original global head (Table A37). All arms pass the initial 85% learning screen. The later expansion criterion requires both CNNs to reach 99% original validation BA in both blocks and the local deficit to stay within 0.5 pp of the global reference. The context CNN in block 2 and the local CNN in block 1 miss that criterion. The phase pilot therefore ends after two blocks.

In the selected local heads, donor-to-original operation-phase exchange changes no probabilities. Restoring all other phase angles produces the same probabilities as restoring only the candidate phase. Among single-channel restorations, replacing the composed writes gives the largest BA gain in both blocks. Restoring decay in the first block also increases BA by 10.42 pp. Table A38 gives all correction and introduced-error counts. These substitutions measure each channel conditional on the other donor channels within each independently fitted head.

All-node local visual reference.

In a separate two-block engineering comparison after the phase pilot, the same CNN trunk projects each local crop to a 384-dimensional vector for the entire Rotary head. It uses no frozen encoder and retains the pilot’s data, 5,040 updates, recurrent-head initialization and validation selection. All 151,026 parameters are in the optimizer. Both CNN and head have nonzero gradients and weight changes. With identical local inputs across the original and donor views, embeddings, phase angles and predictions agree exactly. The original validation BA is 52.53% and 64.03% in the two blocks.

A separate role-wise ridge decoder is fitted on the frozen CNN features with symbol labels and selected on validation. It recovers 5,948 and 5,817 of 6,000 complete validation chains. On the previously examined channel panel it recovers 238 and 234 of 240 programs, with rule BA of 99.58% and 98.33%. The learned head’s low BA coexists with exact paired invariance and high recovery under this readout. Table A39 also gives the four fitted heads’ channel-panel results. The two blocks are drawn from the channel panel, with the exact ten-nonidentity-plus-one-identity subset reported separately. The analysis follows all model and checkpoint selection.

Appendix I Fixed-Layout Whole-Canvas Context

We render a ten-node G5c distractor in rows [0,32)[0,32) of the 112×448112\times 448 canvas. The target occupies rows [32,112)[32,112) with its original query centers at y=56y=56. Distractor draws D0 and D1 follow the same law, use different families, and fully cross distractor legality across the two views and target legality. Candidate siblings share their distractor pair. All target features in a view come from a single encoder pass. The target pixels, query coordinates and sampled patch embeddings are identical across views. The respective vertical patch footprints are [48,64)[48,64) and [42,70)[42,70) for DINOv1 and DINOv2. Sixteen duplicate inputs per block and panel agree exactly at all measured layers. All 24 block-by-panel paired RGB hashes agree across encoders. Across blocks on L7, final-layer feature RMS differences range from 0.662 to 0.714 for DINOv1 and from 0.517 to 0.545 for DINOv2.

For each encoder and head we fit eight models in the same two-row layout using 16,000 training rows, 6,000 validation rows and 5,040 updates per block. Global canonical target-family exclusions separate training, validation and test. Replacement draws preserve the archived training and validation counts by split, nonidentity length, node count and label. The frozen test manifests are released only after checkpoint selection for each encoder. Selected validation BA ranges for Rotary, 2F and GRU are 99.95–100%, 99.98–100% and 99.97–100% with DINOv1 and 89.40–94.98%, 93.98–95.63% and 94.37–95.60% with DINOv2. Role-specific ridge decoders use training and validation only.

Tables A40 and A41 report paired capability, disagreement and phase exchanges. The fixed L7 panel crosses 76 canonical families with eight blocks, two instances per family and both candidate labels. The IID-length L3–7 panel uses 106 reserved short families and approximates the earlier joint length and node-count distribution. The 3-operation row represents one family. The L10 panel has 1,920 disjoint canonical families, two candidate labels per family and no identity operations. The L7 and L10 panels therefore differ in program composition as well as length. In the short panels, 10,000 bootstrap draws resample training blocks and canonical families in crossed fashion and hold the number of families within each length fixed. L10 resamples families nested within blocks. Zero-event resamples describe the observed panel. We report prediction disagreement because both views follow the same law, and the expected directional BA difference is zero. On L7, DINOv2 Rotary’s jointly exact subset has 7.45% disagreement ([5.65,9.38][5.65,9.38]). The all-pair D1-minus-D0 BA difference is +0.33+0.33 pp ([−1.60,+2.26][-1.60,+2.26]). On the 153 jointly exact L7 DINOv2 disagreements, exchanging all phase reproduces the source decision on 60 and 70 pairs in the two directions. Exchanging operation phase alone gives 57 and 50, and exchanging candidate phase alone gives 26 and 15. A semantic control edits only the target candidate, reverses the label in both backgrounds, and keeps the other target pixels fixed. The archive reports capability and correction counts under this edit.

Complementary feature recombination.

A further replay reuses the same two feature sequences and the same fitted heads. We draw eight operation masks per target and mix features from the two scenes with each mask and its complement. The two mixed sequences together use exactly the same feature multiset at each node as the original pair. The start and candidate features remain together in their original view. Masks and their complements contribute to the within-target average before resampling. For DINOv1 Rotary on L10, mixed minus coherent mean BA is −0.0081-0.0081 pp ([−0.1367,+0.1335][-0.1367,+0.1335]). With DINOv2 Rotary on L7, the change is +0.2596+0.2596 pp ([−0.3316,+0.9020][-0.3316,+0.9020]). DINOv2 2F shows small average declines on the IID-length and L10 panels. The replay tests feature mixing over these two backgrounds and shows little BA change for Rotary. Its mixed sequences combine features from the two RGB images.

Appendix J Reproducibility Package

The accompanying REPRODUCIBILITY.md maps every display to its inputs and commands for cached replay, encoding, refits and builds. Manifests retain programs, labels, render seeds and donors. Cached replay needs no download; re-encoding needs the documented encoder weights, and earlier VLM runs need their external weights.

RGB encoding uses float32, channel mean (.485,.456,.406)(.485,.456,.406) and standard deviation (.229,.224,.225)(.229,.224,.225); ordered 384-dimensional query features are stored in float16. Training standardization, threshold 0.5, classwise BA and complete-chain recovery are defined above. Eight-block intervals weight blocks equally; two-block glyph panels report individual observations. The package records software versions, checkpoints, splits and encoder portability checks.
